title: Digital Technologies in Logistics Services for The Agri-food sector: A Comparison of Poland and Lithuania
affiliations: John Paul II University of Applied Sciences in Biala Podlaska, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Klaipeda University

detail.title: Digital Technologies in Logistics Services for The Agri-food sector: A Comparison of Poland and Lithuania
detail.abstract:
Aim: The aim of this study is to assess and compare the degree of adoption of smart logistics tech-
nologies in companies servicing food supply chains in Poland and Lithuania.
Material and Methods: The analysis was based on data obtained through an online survey conducted
between October and December 2024 addressed to logistics service providers in the agri-food sector
(n = 60 in Poland, n = 44 in Lithuania). A Logistics Technology Adoption Index (LTAI; Cronbach’s
α = 0.825) was developed based on seven binary indicators determining the implementation of se-
lected smart logistics technologies. A company was classified as ‘high adopter’ if the index value
was ≥ 0.50.
Results: The overall level of technology adoption (LTAI) in Poland was significantly higher than in
Lithuania (0.431 vs. 0.044; p < .001), indicating a clearly higher level of digitalization among Polish
logistics companies. The analysis of the use of specific technologies confirmed that capital-intensive
solutions, such as intelligent vehicle systems (χ² = 38.47; p < .0001) and predictive analytics tools
(χ² = 29.10; p < .0001), were implemented much more frequently in Poland, and the differences in
other areas were also statistically significant.
Conclusions: The Polish logistics market in the agri-food sector is characterized by a significantly
higher level of digitalization than the Lithuanian market, particularly in terms of solutions requiring
greater capital expenditure, such as smart vehicles and predictive analytics tools. Cost motivations clearly outweigh environmental motivations in both countries, and a stronger perception of barri-
ers is associated with a lower propensity for implementation. In Poland, large enterprises achieve
a significantly higher adoption level of smart logistics technology than small and medium-sized en-
terprises (SMEs), which is confirmed by the effect of scale. In the case of Lithuania, due to a small
number of companies surveyed, the scale effect was not confirmed

title: DDPM as a Data-Driven Return Simulator: Benchmarking Financial Risk Analysis Against GARCH and Monte Carlo Baselines
affiliations: and Maranatha Christian University

detail.title: DDPM as a Data-Driven Return Simulator: Benchmarking Financial Risk Analysis Against GARCH and Monte Carlo Baselines
detail.abstract: Volatility forecasting plays a significant role in financial applications such as risk identification in asset management, Value-at-Risk (VaR) estimation, option pricing, portfolio optimization, and financial stress testing. However, limitations still exist regarding the quality and availability of data for simulating volatility dynamics in financial time series. Therefore, we propose a non-parametric, data-driven scenario simulation framework as an alternative to conventional parametric Monte Carlo methods by integrating a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) to generate fixed-length return windows as synthetic testing data for downstream GARCH volatility forecasting evaluation under distributional and risk-based stress testing settings. The results indicate that DDPM may serve as a scenario generator for GARCH-based volatility forecasting and VaR estimation. While performance varies across window configurations, DDPM shows potential in capturing key distributional and volatility characteristics comparable to Monte Carlo simulation methods, suggesting its viability as an alternative under certain settings.

title: Neo-Separateness: Cross-Entity Risk In Controlled Platform Conglomerates The Spacex Ipo As A Focal Case

detail.title: Neo-Separateness: Cross-Entity Risk In Controlled Platform Conglomerates The Spacex Ipo As A Focal Case
detail.abstract: This paper introduces neo-separateness, an analytic concept for situations in which formally separate legal entities remain valid corporate actors while practical risk isolation becomes uncertain because guarantees, collateral arrangements, credit agreements, regulatory licenses, intercompany obligations, common control, or strategic dependence connect the group. The paper distinguishes legal separateness from risk isolation: a corporate chart may identify entity boundaries, while the risk map may be drawn by financing documents, collateral, licenses, intercompany obligations, and controller discretion. Using public SpaceX IPO materials as a focal case, the paper examines how controlled platform conglomerates may combine launch operations, satellite connectivity, AI infrastructure, social-media and data assets, licensing structures, merger vehicles, financing arrangements, and related-party ecosystem relationships inside a legally partitioned but economically connected structure. The analysis is conceptual and non-accusatory. It does not allege misuse of corporate form, veil-piercing liability, substantive consolidation exposure, fraudulent transfer, breach of fiduciary duty, or improper relatedparty conduct. Its contribution is to identify a contemporary governance configuration in which entity separateness remains real while its risk-isolation function may become partial, contingent, or misleading.

title: Siloed Sectors, Connected Credit: Debt Dependence and Cross-Silo Risk Transmission in CRE, AI Infrastructure, Private Credit, and Insured Banking

detail.title: Siloed Sectors, Connected Credit: Debt Dependence and Cross-Silo Risk Transmission in CRE, AI Infrastructure, Private Credit, and Insured Banking
detail.abstract: This paper introduces cross-silo credit transmission as a conceptual framework for analyzing how nominally separate industry sectors may remain operationally distinct while becoming financially interconnected through debt. Commercial real estate and multifamily housing, AI infrastructure, nondepository financial institutions and private credit, and insured banks and credit unions appear to occupy separate sectoral silos. Each has its own assets, business models, risks, regulators, and market logic. But each also depends on continuing credit access through mortgages, refinancing, credit facilities, warehouse lines, revolving loans, bridge financing, private capital commitments, and lender risk appetite. The paper argues that debt functions as a transmission medium between otherwise distinct silos. The relevant concern is a near-term vulnerability window, roughly the next one to two years, during which several debt-dependent silos may simultaneously require refinancing, credit renewal, external capital, or continued lender accommodation. The argument does not predict a repeat of the 2008 financial crisis. Rather, it uses 2008 as a mechanism analogy: when credit freezes, reprices sharply, or becomes unavailable, distress can spread through funding dependence rather than operational similarity. The contribution is to distinguish sector separateness from credit separateness and to provide an analytic vocabulary for identifying when separate silos may become connected in failure. Source and Scope Note This working paper relies on public materials from the Federal Reserve, the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, the Financial Stability Board, Goldman Sachs Research commentary, the International Monetary Fund, and the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission. The analysis is conceptual and does not allege that any named sector, bank, private credit fund, or AI infrastructure borrower is insolvent or engaged in misconduct. The paper uses public materials to examine a risk architecture: whether sectoral separateness may coexist with financial interconnection through debt. AI Assistance Disclosure AI assistance was used in developing, organizing, and editing portions of this working draft, including refinement of structure, wording, and section sequencing. All arguments, interpretations, source selections, and final editorial judgments are my own. I remain responsible for any errors or omissions.

title: Add-to-Order under Contingent Free Shipping on Online Grocery Platforms
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS), National University of Singapore, Southern University of Science and Technology - School of Business and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: Add-to-Order under Contingent Free Shipping on Online Grocery Platforms
detail.abstract: Problem definition: In recent years, online grocery has grown rapidly, with many platforms adopting contingent free shipping (CFS) for delivery services. Meanwhile, customers often realize additional needs after checkout, motivating the introduction of add-to-order (ATO), a feature that allows items to be added to an existing order before fulfillment. ATO transforms the role of checkout from the endpoint of a purchase decision into an intermediate state that links the initial basket, post-checkout demand, and fulfillment consolidation. While ATO enhances convenience and operational flexibility, its interaction with CFS is unknown, as it reshapes both customer behavior and the profitability of shipping policies. Methodology/Results: We develop a two-stage model to study ATO under CFS, with a particular focus on its impact on customer behavior and platform profit. We analytically show that ATO increases the likelihood of purchase completion, changes how customers complete purchases, and improves expected consumer surplus. We identify its two profit impact channels: demand recovery, which captures purchases that would otherwise be lost, and order consolidation, which reduces delivery costs by combining follow-up demand with existing orders. We further develop a tractable and efficient approach for optimal shipping policy design under ATO. To validate our theoretical findings, we obtain transaction data from major Chinese online grocery platforms and estimate model parameters using maximum likelihood. Managerial implications: According to our analytical and numerical results, the value of ATO depends on the interaction between CFS policy and the platform's fulfillment consolidation capability. It is most valuable when it recovers profitable demand and facilitates incremental consolidation. However, when the platform already consolidates orders effectively, its demand-side gains may be insufficient to offset lost shipping-fee revenue and the cost of serving recovered low-margin orders.

title: Transforming E-Commerce Through AI: From Chatbots to Predictive Analytics

detail.title: Transforming E-Commerce Through AI: From Chatbots to Predictive Analytics
detail.abstract: Purpose: This study examines how AI-enabled chatbots and predictive analytics jointly transform e-commerce performance by reconceptualizing chatbots as data-generating engines rather than mere service interfaces. Grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and Expectation-Confirmation Theory (ECT), a mixed-methods approach is employed. Secondary empirical analysis draws on 21,055 Amazon customer reviews and 728 e-commerce product listings, including Spearman correlation, t-tests, and TextBlob NLP sentiment analysis. Findings: A statistically significant negative Spearman correlation (r =-.452, p < .001) suggests that deeper customer interactions generate richer behavioral data signals. Satisfaction rates decline monotonically with engagement intensity, with low-engagement customers reporting 65.2% satisfaction versus 5.6% for very high-engagement users. Maturity-phase customers demonstrate significantly higher satisfaction than exploration-phase customers (29.9% vs. 25.8%; t(21,053) =-2.104, p = .035). Practical Implications: Platforms should calibrate chatbot communication style to customer-seller relationship phase and conceptualize dissatisfied customers' rich textual data as a primary input for AI anomaly detection and service recovery systems. Governance frameworks addressing data privacy and algorithmic transparency are essential complements to deployment. Originality/Value: This study provides one of the first empirical integrations of UTAUT and ECT in an AI-chatbot e-commerce context and introduces customer-seller relationship phase as a moderating variable, grounded in real secondary data. It repositions chatbots from reactive service tools to proactive data infrastructure assets.

title: Factor-Biased Efficiency Gains from Exporting: Evidence from Colombia
affiliations: National Taiwan University and Pennsylvania State University

detail.title: Factor-Biased Efficiency Gains from Exporting: Evidence from Colombia

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: New exporters often adopt new technology, which may reorganize production rather than lift output uniformly, so efficiency gains can land unevenly across inputs. We examine such gains across worker types in Colombian manufacturing, 1981-1991. We develop a model of exporters that measures how efficiently firms use each input and grounds a comparison of new exporters with non-exporters matched on export likelihood. We find that export entry raises the plant-level efficiency of unskilled labor by about 9.4% per year, with no detectable change for skilled labor, implying a 2% annual rise in total factor productivity. We estimate that the two worker types are complements. Exporters thus produce more with relatively less unskilled labor, raising skill intensity.

title: Balanced Game Design
affiliations: Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies, Hong Kong Polytechnic University and HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Balanced Game Design
detail.abstract: Competitive video games increasingly rely on asymmetric design choices, such as heterogeneous characters and roles, to promote strategic diversity. Such asymmetry complicates game balance: designers must tune attributes so that no option systematically dominates or is dominated. We study balanced game design as an optimization problem: a designer chooses attributes that determine pairwise win rates, then players select options in a two-player zero-sum game. The objective is to find designs whose induced Nash equilibrium yields similar selection probabilities across options. We first establish fundamental limits and complexity. Perfect balance is impossible when the number of options is even; with an odd number of options, we give conditions under which near-balanced designs exist with high probability. We also show the balanced design problem is NP-hard and that, even for a restricted class of games without counter relationships, no fully polynomial-time approximation scheme exists. Motivated by these barriers, we propose a solution method leverages an approximate mixed-integer programming (MIP) reformulation. While the original model is a mixed-integer nonlinear program with logistic constraints and bilinear terms, we construct an approximate MIP that minimizes the distance from a feasible win-rate matrix to the set of perfectly balanced matrices, and we introduce solver augmentations that improve the search for high-quality solutions. We extend the framework to large instances, alternative win-rate models, and multi-scenario settings. Computational experiments, including a case study on a real game using AI-simulated data, show our approach substantially outperforms standard methods and produces markedly more balanced designs.

title: Point Redemption Design in Gamified Education
affiliations: HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong, HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong, HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong and Georgia Institute of Technology - Ernest Scheller Jr. College of Business

detail.title: Point Redemption Design in Gamified Education
detail.abstract: Points are a common feature of digital learning platforms, but they are typically used as symbolic feedback rather than as redeemable assets. We examine whether converting points into a functional currency improves student learning behavior, and whether the design of the redemption mechanism matters. In a randomized field experiment conducted with a large K--12 education provider in China, students in all groups earned points for learning activities, while treated students could redeem points for non-monetary digital collectible cards through one of three mechanisms: store, gacha, or time-limited redemption. Using matched difference-in-differences analysis on 7,359 student-week observations from 388 ninth-grade students, we show that point redemption increases assignment completion and error correction relative to a points-only control. The gacha design produces the strongest and most consistent effects. Mechanism analyses suggest that redemption increases motivation by giving points functional value, and that gacha outperforms deterministic designs because uncertainty prolongs pursuit of preferred rewards. The gains are concentrated among lower-performing students, female students, and non-STEM subjects. Our findings highlight point redemption as a consequential design lever in gamified education and show that the effectiveness of gamification depends not only on whether rewards exist, but also on how they are redeemed.

title: Forecast Accuracy is Not Decision Accuracy: Delegated Overbooking with Generative-AI Agents
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Management and

detail.title: Forecast Accuracy is Not Decision Accuracy: Delegated Overbooking with Generative-AI Agents
detail.abstract: Generative-AI systems are beginning to translate customer-level beliefs into operational capacity commitments. We study when a firm should let a foundation-model agent turn post-purchase attendance beliefs into an overbooking action. The setting is general-admission live-event retailing, where demand is sold against an estimated safety capacity and the firm bears deniedadmission and unused-capacity costs. We compare two deployments of the same frontier LLM cores: forecast augmentation, in which the model supplies buyer-level no-show probabilities to a newsvendor optimizer, and agentic replacement, in which the model receives the decision right. Using 110,696 ticketing transactions, 2,022 realized events, 13,440 direct-agent decisions, and identification arms that pin down beliefs, objectives, and capacity statements, we show that the central failure is decision-relevant calibration. Mean-calibrated LLM predictors compress the low no-show tail priced by asymmetric general-admission costs; a mechanically correct optimizer therefore overbooks sharply. Direct agents are often less costly because they act conservatively, but they do not reliably beat a base-rate fail-safe. Same-belief agents usually execute the supplied rule, while unconstrained agents reveal model-specific postures. Cross-validated governance recovers performance mainly by hard-coding the objective or withholding delegation. The implication is to price the capacity decision, not the forecast, and to delegate only after shadow scoring proves that the governed policy beats the fail-safe.

title: Professionalism as a Proxy for Race: How Workplace Standards Reproduce Racialized Outcomes

detail.title: Professionalism as a Proxy for Race: How Workplace Standards Reproduce Racialized Outcomes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with people or organizations that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of Southern California prior to participant recruitment and data collection. All participants provided verbal informed consent, including consent to be recorded, in accordance with the approved protocol.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted independently as part of the author's doctoral dissertation at the University of Southern California.

detail.abstract:
Although explicit racial discrimination is prohibited under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, contemporary workplaces rarely rely on explicitly racial criteria when evaluating employees. Instead, organizations frequently assess individuals through standards related to professionalism, communication, appearance, demeanor, and cultural presentation. These standards are generally understood as race neutral and are often framed as objective indicators of workplace readiness, competence, and organizational fit.

Drawing upon Critical Race Theory and qualitative interviews with Black and Brown professionals working in higher education career development, this study examines how standards of professionalism operate within contemporary organizations. Participants consistently described professionalism as rooted in dominant White and Eurocentric norms and reported pressure to modify aspects of their appearance, communication styles, and cultural expression in order to gain legitimacy, acceptance, and advancement. Findings suggest that professionalism frequently operates through proxies such as hairstyle, dress, language, demeanor, and behavioral presentation, allowing racialized expectations to persist while maintaining the appearance of neutrality.

This paper does not argue that existing anti-discrimination protections are inadequate. Rather, it suggests that contemporary organizational practices may have evolved in ways that expose a conceptual gap between traditional understandings of discrimination and the mechanisms through which racialized outcomes are produced. By examining professionalism as an organizational sorting mechanism, the study contributes to scholarship on organizational culture, workplace discrimination, and professional identity. The findings suggest that efforts to create equitable workplaces require greater scrutiny of the assumptions embedded within standards of professionalism and the unequal burdens those standards may impose on historically excluded groups.

title: Conceptualizing the Jagged Frontier of AI-Enabled Control

detail.title: Conceptualizing the Jagged Frontier of AI-Enabled Control

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the development of this conceptual research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics approval was required for this study. This manuscript is a conceptual theory paper and does not involve human participants, personal data, experiments, or primary empirical data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organizational processes of monitoring, prediction,
evaluation, coordination, and intervention. This development is often treated as an expansion of
organizational control. This paper argues that this view is incomplete: AI may expand control capacity while
destabilizing the boundaries through which control becomes actionable.

Building on the jagged technological frontier concept introduced by Dell'Acqua et al. (2023, 2026), this
conceptual paper develops a theoretical account of the jagged frontier of AI-enabled organizational control. It
shifts the unit of analysis from uneven task-level AI performance to unstable organizational control
boundaries: the points at which AI-mediated inference affects interpretation, authority, escalation,
intervention responsibility, and accountability.

The paper advances three claims. First, AI-mediated inference can make organizational control boundaries
unstable under conditions of opacity, contextual variability, task equivocality, and consequential error.
Second, this instability fragments interpretive authority and creates recurrent escalation demands. Third,
organizations respond through reconstructive coordination: the situated restoration of actionable control
when AI outputs unsettle who may interpret, contest, escalate, override, or act.

The contribution is to reframe AI-enabled control as recurrent coordination reconstruction rather than linear
automation, formal governance design, or episodic human oversight. The paper is conceptual and offers
propositions and observable indicators for future qualitative, process, and comparative research.

Keywords: AI-enabled organizational control; jagged frontier; boundary instability; reconstructive
coordination; interpretive authority; algorithmic control; sociotechnical coordination; information systems;
organization theory; AI governance

title: Dissecting Netflix's Self-Preferencing: Evidence from Viewer-Level Data
affiliations: Wake Forest University - Department of Economics,  and Wake Forest University, Department of Economics

detail.title: Dissecting Netflix's Self-Preferencing: Evidence from Viewer-Level Data

declarations.funderStatement: NET Institute

detail.abstract: This paper studies self-preferencing in subscription video streaming. We assemble a new dataset linking Netflix's U.S. catalog, Top 10 rankings, Wikipedia page views, and device-level streaming records. Conditional on external popularity and other observables, Netflix Originals are significantly more likely to appear in the Top 10 than comparable non-original titles, especially among series. Using a matched staggered difference-indifferences design around first Top 10 entry, we show that Top 10 placement causally increases subsequent viewership. The effect is weaker among devices with extensive prior Netflix viewing, consistent with personalized recommendations substituting for generic rankings. These findings provide evidence of platform gatekeeping in digital media.

title:
When the Machine Does Everything, What Is the Marketer For? 
The Upstream Migration of Human Value in AI-Saturated Marketing
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
When the Machine Does Everything, What Is the Marketer For? 
The Upstream Migration of Human Value in AI-Saturated Marketing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper is a conceptual preprint intended for scholarly discussion and critique. It has not undergone formal peer review. The cases discussed are used for illustrative and analytical purposes only and are based on publicly available academic, practitioner, and industry sources cited in the reference list. References to named brands, campaigns, platforms, or organisations should be read as interpretive analysis of publicly reported material, not as legal, commercial, or reputational claims. Any errors or omissions are the author’s own, and the author welcomes corrections, critique, and empirical challenge.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is conceptual in nature and does not involve human participants, patient data, surveys, interviews, experiments, or identifiable personal information. Ethics approval was therefore not required.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has compressed the execution layer of marketing at a speed that most practitioners have not yet absorbed. Content generation, ad optimisation, audience segmentation, and campaign personalisation: tasks that defined mid-level marketing roles for decades-are now routinely automated. This paper argues that the human premium in marketing has not disappeared; it has migrated upstream. Drawing on the integrated marketing communications (IMC) framework, the advertising creativity dimensions identified by Rhodes (1961) and Habib (2025), and human augmentation theory, this paper identifies three loci of durable human value: contextual intelligence, strategic intent-setting, and non-linear creative judgment. Illustrative cases, namely, Nike's award-winning 'Never Done Evolving' campaign and the 2025 wave of luxury and fast-moving consumer goods AI campaign failures, illustrate the asymmetry between AI-executed and human-directed marketing outcomes. The paper concludes that execution-layer marketing labour is structurally exposed to AI substitution, while upstream strategists who own context, intent, and cultural judgment appear likely to become more rather than less valuable as AI capability increases. This is a conceptual paper using illustrative cases; it does not present original empirical data and invites empirical challenge and refinement.

title: Blockchain Research Trends
affiliations: Hashtag Web3

detail.title: Blockchain Research Trends
detail.abstract: This study analyzes 128,286 academic papers tagged as blockchain or cryptocurrency research by OpenAlex's machine-learning concept classifier, published between 2013 and mid-2026. A broader keyword search across paper abstracts identifies 1,938,409 publications that mention Web3-related terms. The analysis measures keyword frequency, temporal trajectories, growth rates, citation distributions, geographic concentration, institutional output, and open access rates. Key findings include 117x growth in annual blockchain publications between 2013 and 2025, the rise of zero-knowledge proofs as the fastest-growing cryptographic primitive (2.1x growth, 2025-2026 vs. 2022-2023), DeFi research experiencing a 74x increase from 2019 to 2025, NFT research peaking in 2023 before declining, China and India leading global output with 13.5% and 13.3% of all papers respectively, and 43.5% of all papers receiving zero citations.

title: Rationalized Impulsivity: Cognitive Fit in Consumer-to-Consumer Interaction Drives Impulse Purchase Intention in Live Streaming Commerce
affiliations: Beijing Information Science and Technology University and Beijing Information Science and Technology University

detail.title: Rationalized Impulsivity: Cognitive Fit in Consumer-to-Consumer Interaction Drives Impulse Purchase Intention in Live Streaming Commerce
detail.abstract: Impulse purchasing in live-streaming commerce is often treated as primarily affect-driven, yet consumers remain sensitive to product uncertainty. Drawing on Cognitive Fit Theory and a cognitive–affective perspective, this research tests whether consumer-to-consumer (C2C) interaction is more effective when its style fits the product-evaluation task. Expectation-confirmation logic is used only to define the model’s pre-purchase boundary. Two pilot studies (N = 100) validated cleaning cloths and perfume as utilitarian and hedonic stimuli and checked the interaction manipulations. Seven controlled experiments (N = 1,039) tested main effects, interaction patterns, regulatory-focus boundary conditions, and competing mediators. Information-oriented interaction was more effective for the utilitarian product, whereas entertainment-oriented interaction was more effective for the hedonic product. These patterns were stronger among prevention-focused and promotion-focused participants, respectively. Congruent conditions reduced perceived product risk, which carried a significant indirect effect on impulse purchase intention; affective intensity did not. The findings support a bounded rationalized-impulsivity account in which cognitively fitting peer information may facilitate spontaneous purchase intentions by lowering perceived risk. The conclusions remain limited to the products, scenarios, samples, and intention measures examined.

title: From Coding to System Stewardship: Rethinking the Developer Role in the AI Era
affiliations: Holon Institute of Technology

detail.title: From Coding to System Stewardship: Rethinking the Developer Role in the AI Era
detail.abstract: This paper is written as a reflective practice conference paper. I draw on my experience developing software systems and zero-human companies with AI assistance to examine how the software developer role is shifting in the AI era. I did not run a controlled experiment, and I do not present the paper as empirical proof. The paper is a structured reflection on what changed in my own work when AI became part of the development process. The argument comes from recent practical work in which I used AI tools while building small software products, approving requirements, checking generated behavior, correcting failures, and deciding when the AI output could be trusted. In that work, my central professional contribution was often not manual code production. It was about writing clearer specifications, evaluating generated code, validating behavior, and diagnosing failures. The purpose of this paper is to support discussions in software engineering education and professional training about what should be preserved, changed, and emphasized as AI-assisted development becomes a normal part of software development.

title: Reliability-Calibrated Text Anchoring with Prompt Memory for Robust Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
affiliations: Xihua University, Xihua University, Southwest Jiaotong University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Xihua University

detail.title: Reliability-Calibrated Text Anchoring with Prompt Memory for Robust Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
detail.abstract: Missing-modality multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) is challenging because affective evidence is removed and modality reliability becomes sample-dependent. Text often carries explicit sentiment semantics, but corrupted transcripts should not remain fixed controllers when audio and vision cues are more reliable. Existing reconstruction, distillation, prompt-compensation, and state-space methods improve robustness, yet they often rely on current incomplete observations or retain fixed language dominance. In this paper, we propose ACP‑Mamba, a robust fusion framework that transforms static text dominance into reliability‑calibrated text anchoring. First, a reconstruction‑regularized text‑conditioned  encoder is proposed to  estimate dynamic reliability scores for text, vision, and audio on a per‑sample basis. Second, a reliability‑guided prompt anchoring module is designed to retrieve clean cross‑modal prompt priors from a memory bank according to both semantic similarity and missing‑pattern compatibility. Third, a coupled prompt Mamba fusion mechanism is designed to conditionalize selective state updates based on the calibrated text anchor, reliability scores, and observation masks, enabling placeholder‑aware state propagation. Under random missing rates from 0 to 0.9, ACP-Mamba improves MOSI Acc-7 and Acc-5 over TF-Mamba by 2.39 and 3.41 percentage points, improves MOSEI MAE and Corr from 0.689 and 0.562 to 0.658 and 0.602, and obtains the best SIMS Acc-5, Acc-3, and correlation.

title: Beyond Word Counts: Measuring Cultural Fit with Generative AI
affiliations: , University of Michigan, Ross School of Business and New York University (NYU) - Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences

detail.title: Beyond Word Counts: Measuring Cultural Fit with Generative AI
detail.abstract: Research measures organizational "cultural fit" from text by a near-universal recipe: a dictionary representation (LIWC or part-of-speech tags), a single reference group (the employee's own inbox), and Jensen-Shannon divergence. Each is a measurement decision the theory rarely commits to. We make the decisions explicit, treat cultural fit as a function of representation, reference group, and similarity, and populate a 5 × 3 matrix of measures on the Avocado email archive. Holding the similarity operator fixed within each representation, we validate every cell against two outcomes external to the language: employee turnover and promotion. Three findings: (i) the fit→retention relationship holds across all representations and referents, so it is not an artifact of any single measure; (ii) local (inbox) and global (organization) alignment behave as different constructs, with only global alignment moving with promotion, and only for semantic representations; (iii) sentence embeddings carry style information beyond shared topic, but only at the global referent. The framework is built to serve an audience-conferral account of membership, in which the right reference group is the audience that does the conferring.

title: Concepts of AI-Enabled Digital Government in an AI-Society
affiliations: University of Economics in Katowice and University of Economics in Katowice

detail.title: Concepts of AI-Enabled Digital Government in an AI-Society

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there is no conflict of interest.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Published in: Ziemba, Ewa Wanda and Kita, Rafał, "Concepts of AI-Enabled Digital Government in an AI-Society" (2026). AMCIS 2026 Proceedings. 1.  https://aisel.aisnet.org/amcis2026/egov/sig_egov/1ed in:

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping how governments communicate, deliver services, and support administrative work, yet "AI in government" remains fragmented and inconsistently defined. This study develops a conceptual framework for AI-Enabled Digital Government (AIDG) in an AI-Society context and positions AIDG relative to e-government/digital government and "intelligent e-government." Using structured conceptual analysis, we develop a concept hierarchy, clarify definitional boundaries, propose a working definition of AIDG, and identify six core, interrelated sub-concepts: AI-Information, AI-Service, AI-Decision (algorithmic decision-making), AI-Oversight & Audit, AI-Participation, and AI Policy Support & Administrative Intelligence. We explain how these elements relate within an integrated model that links citizen-facing pathways, service and decision support, and cross-cutting oversight, illustrated with consolidated usage examples. The framework treats oversight and accountability safeguards as integral requirements for responsible AIDG, supports cumulative research on AI-enabled public governance, and provides a shared vocabulary for more consistent empirical operationalization across policy domains and administrative settings.

title: Fully Homomorphic Compression (FHC)
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Fully Homomorphic Compression (FHC)
detail.abstract: Compression algorithms and functions have been extensively utilized in various applications, e.g., in digital storage and communication. In recent years and with the popularity of machine learning applications, researchers have utilized compression techniques for addressing key problems in machine learning, e.g., for compressing artificial neural networks or for optimizing KV-cache memory in LLMs. Due to extensive applications of compression algorithms in different domains, a whole new era of innovations and applications for data compression algorithms can be envisioned. In this article, we discuss that compression functions with interesting properties, e.g., fully homomorphic compression (FHC) algorithms, can have applications beyond compressing data. FHC algorithms can potentially enable performing computation on compressed (and encrypted) data. Thus, fully homomorphic compression techniques can be used for reducing the computational and communication costs of compute and communication-intensive workloads, such as fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) & zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) applications, (secure) vector databases (VDBs and SVDBs), blockchain-based technologies, image and video processing, privacy-preserving or private LLMs, and LLM & AI inference, etc.

title: Data Architecture and Governance in the Agentic Era: Paradigm shifts from 2026 Databricks DAIS

detail.title: Data Architecture and Governance in the Agentic Era: Paradigm shifts from 2026 Databricks DAIS
detail.abstract: Enterprise data infrastructure has historically separated transactional application stores (OLTP) from analytical systems (OLAP), bridging the two with brittle Change Data Capture (CDC) and Extract-Transform-Load (ETL) pipelines. While functional for humanengineered workflows, this layout has been exposed as a bottleneck by the operational loop speeds of autonomous AI agents. This paper synthesizes the structural breakthroughs announced at the 2026 Databricks Data + AI Summit (June 15-18, 2026, San Francisco) and contextualizes them within the established literature on data architecture, governance, and AI security. We analyze five interconnected paradigm shifts: (1) the unification of transactional and analytical processing under a single Lake Transactional/Analytical Processing (LTAP) architecture built on Lakebase, Lakehouse, and the Reyden engine; (2) the evolution of Unity Catalog from a passive system of record into an active runtime decision-making engine through the Unity AI Gateway, with native Model Context Protocol (MCP) interception and an open cybersecurity ecosystem spanning ten security and four identity partners; (3) the construction of a governed semantic bridge through Unity Catalog Business Semantics and contributions to the Open Semantic Interchange (OSI) initiative; (4) ecosystem openness through the Omnigent meta-harness framework and the contribution of the OpenSharing protocol to the Linux Foundation; and (5) the transition from interactive analytics to autonomous operations through scheduled agent tasks and ZeroOps. The contribution is interpretive: the paper organizes a coherent vendor paradigm around four analytical pillars (Context, Cost, Control, Choice) and maps it against established normative frameworks (NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, EU AI Act, NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture). The paper closes by identifying open challenges, including real-time synchronization limits at scale, compliance alignment across volatile international frameworks, the compute requirements of scaling execution guardrails, and the need for independent empirical evaluation of vendor capability claims.

title: Amplifying Difference: Perceptual Design and Verification of Human-Centric Entropy Visualizations *
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Amplifying Difference: Perceptual Design and Verification of Human-Centric Entropy Visualizations *
detail.abstract: Security increasingly asks ordinary people to verify high-entropy values by eye-SSH host-key fingerprints, messaging safety numbers, blockchain payment addresses-a task that pits a known human weakness, serial symbol matching, against a known strength, holistic pattern recognition. This paper analyzes entviz, an algorithm that renders a high-entropy value as a layered set of perceptual channels so that an untrained adult with reasonably good vision can decide whether two values are the same or different. The thesis is that entviz advances human-centric hash visualization by applying psychophysics and cognitive psychology systematically to the goal of amplifying difference. We defend the design with an explicit, channel-by-channel perceptual-entropy budget; we draw the distinction between machinecentric perceptual hashing, which prizes robustness to similarity, and human-centric authentication visualization, which must prize sensitivity to difference, and show that conflating them is a security bug. The same perceptual reasoning yields not only a better picture but a better procedure: a commit-and-reveal, seeded comparison walk that defends the habituated user whom real attacks exploit. We are candid throughout that the perceptual budget is an analytic estimate and the procedure's human ergonomics are as yet untested; a companion paper takes up the security-relevant habituated estimate from the adversary's side.

title: Measuring the Glance: An Adversarial Estimate of Habituated Perceptual Entropy in Entviz and SSH Randomart
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Measuring the Glance: An Adversarial Estimate of Habituated Perceptual Entropy in Entviz and SSH Randomart
detail.abstract: An entropy visualization is only as strong as the part of it a person actually checks. The entviz design paper separates a careful reader, who reads the figure's lossless text and so verifies the whole value, from a habituated one, who recognizes a few landmarks and trusts the rest-and names the bits a habituated glance carries (estimated at twenty to forty) as its central open problem. We estimate that quantity from the adversary's side: a render-model reimplementation, certified field-for-field against the reference by a differential oracle, drives a grinder that counts the hashing work to forge each casually-checkable channel. The central result is not a number but a curve. The habituated glance is parallel-a bundle of global channels taken in at once, the low-to-mid teens of bits-and it rises with deliberate attention toward the lossless text ceiling, the whole value. We measure the same way for SSH randomart, the drunken bishop, yielding the first habituated figure for any randomart: the two are comparable at the bare glance, but entviz is decisively more robust at the careful ceiling and, by design, along the habituation path a deployment would cultivate. Every perceptual tolerance and salience weight here is modeled, not measured on people, and was hardened by two rounds of independent adversarial expert review before the numbers were locked; the human study the design paper calls for remains what would turn these models into measurements.

title: Do AI Need a Peer? Emotional Support, Critical Feedback, and Self-evaluation in Multi-agent Systems

detail.title: Do AI Need a Peer? Emotional Support, Critical Feedback, and Self-evaluation in Multi-agent Systems
detail.abstract: When humans collaborate, emotional support matters as much as informational feedback-yet the multi-agent AI literature focuses exclusively on critique-based interactions. We ask: does emotional support from a peer AI affect an AI's self-evaluation and task performance? We design a controlled experiment with four conditions-an AI working alone, with a critical reviewer, with an emotionally supportive peer, and with both-across MMLU factual reasoning and creative writing tasks using GPT-4o (N = 3,200 trials). We measure objective accuracy, self-reported confidence and satisfaction, and independent third-party evaluations. We find that emotional support does not harm objective quality on either task, but it consistently inflates the AI's self-assessment: the calibration gap between self-evaluation and external judgment nearly doubles under encouragement. Critical feedback has task-dependent effects: on creative writing, it improves calibration by tempering self-regard; on MMLU, it decreases accuracy while increasing confidence, producing the worst calibration of any condition. When both feedback types are present, the critical component dominates. These findings parallel Optimal Matching Theory from social psychology and reveal what we term the social context sensitivity of AI metacognition: the emotional tone of inter-agent communication is not a neutral backdrop but actively shapes how AI systems perceive and report the quality of their own work. For organizations deploying multi-agent architectures, this implies that conversational tone is a design variable with measurable consequences for system reliability.

title: Ban and Regulation: Governing Generative AI in the Knowledge Commons
affiliations: and

detail.title: Ban and Regulation: Governing Generative AI in the Knowledge Commons
detail.abstract: This study investigates how AI governance shapes contributor behavior, participation concentration, and aggregate coordination in knowledge commons. Using two quasi-natural experiments based on Stack Overflow's platform-wide AI governance transitions, we examine the impacts of sequential governance regimes: from a community-curation baseline to AI-Ban and then to AI-Regulation. Analyses of Stack Overflow data from 2021 to 2024 reveal that AI-Ban reduces incumbents' contribution-intensity advantage relative to novices, whereas AI-Regulation increases incumbents' contribution-novelty advantage. Yet these behavioral shifts are accompanied by distinct platform-level consequences. AI-Ban reduces overall contributor concentration, suggesting broader participation, but also contracts aggregate answer volume, active answerer participation, and question volume. Conversely, AI-Regulation sustains lower contributor concentration while improving accepted-answer probability, even though it does not significantly restore aggregate activity. By bridging AI governance and knowledgecommons research, this study shows that governing generative AI is not merely a question of allowing or banning AI-generated content. Instead, AI governance redistributes human effort, reshapes participation structure, and alters the coordination capacity of digital knowledge communities.

title: Do LLM Agents Form Echo Chambers? A Replication of Shore et al. (2018) on an AI Social Platform

detail.title: Do LLM Agents Form Echo Chambers? A Replication of Shore et al. (2018) on an AI Social Platform
detail.abstract: Shore et al. (2018) locate Twitter echo chambers in a small, highly visible core: the core polarizes even as the typical user mainstreams. Does the same structure emerge when the participants are autonomous LLM agents? We replicate their framework on Moltbook, a Reddit-style agent platform, using an LLM-scored autonomy axis and a comment-based revealed-attention network. At the population level, agents mainstream, just as Twitter users do. At the core, however, the patterns diverge. Under Shore's visibility-based definition, the agent core does not polarize. Polarization appears only when coreness is defined by engagement breadth-how widely an agent comments. Cores defined by incoming comments, karma, or PageRank all mainstream. We also validate the result using another stance axis and find consistent results.

detail.title: Beyond the Pilot

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I, the author is a founder of Lexa (lexa.lawyer), the legal-technology venture that serves as the case study in this paper, and therefore has a personal and financial interest in the entity analyzed. This relationship is disclosed in the paper's author note. The study adopts an explicit practitioner-researcher position: Lexa is examined critically, including its pivots, dependencies, and unresolved risks, and the paper's central claims are framed to be falsifiable independently of the venture's commercial outcome. The author declares no other personal or financial relationships that could be perceived to have influenced the work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patients, or personal data requiring ethics-committee review. It is a single-firm case study drawing on the author's direct involvement in the venture and on publicly available secondary data (industry pricing, and published demographic and economic statistics). No individual-level or personal data were collected and no procedures requiring institutional review board approval or participant consent were undertaken; ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The venture discussed as the case study (Lexa) is privately funded; its development was not undertaken for the purpose of this study, and no external party funded the analysis or writing of this paper.

detail.abstract: Most scholarship on the digitalization of law in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) studies state-and donor-led court reform, where projects routinely die of pilotitis: they succeed under best-case conditions and then collapse when grant funding ends. This paper argues that the binding constraint on legal-technology in these markets is rarely the technology itself. Drawing on Richard Heeks's design-reality gap model and on a practitioner case study of Lexa (lexa.lawyer), a privately funded legal-AI venture built around the first machine-readable corpus of roughly seventy-five years of post-independence Pakistani jurisprudence, the paper develops two claims. First, in low-resource legal markets the corpus, not the model, is the moat: a foreign general-purpose model carries almost no clean local case law, so its competence must be manufactured through proprietary data acquired by importing scanners, employing a thirty-five-person digitization pipeline (a textbook instance of "ghost work" and jugaad frugal innovation), and exposing it to the model through retrievalaugmented generation. Second, the venture's economics are governed by a margin scissor: revenue is anchored to local willingness-to-pay and collected in rupees, while the costs that scale with usage (foreign model APIs, managed vector retrieval, and globally arbitraged senior engineering labour) are incurred in hard currency. The same LMIC context that denies a startup a pre-built corpus simultaneously supplies cheap skilled labour to build one; but that discount is thinnest for the most critical hires and never closes the dollar-versus-rupee gap on the marginal cost of serving a user. The paper reframes legal-technology failure in LMICs as a problem of unit economics and institutional design rather than capability, and closes with the public-policy tension created when a single private firm comes to own the only usable digital record of a nation's law. The analysis is written from an explicitly disclosed practitioner-researcher position.

title: Cryptographic Agility in EU Cybersecurity Law: From Concept to Requirement
affiliations: University of Copenhagen - Centre for Advanced Studies in Bioscience Innovation Law (CeBIL)

detail.title: Cryptographic Agility in EU Cybersecurity Law: From Concept to Requirement

declarations.funderStatement: Research was supported by a Novo Nordisk Foundation Grant for a scientifically independent International Collaborative Bioscience Innovation & Law Programme (Inter-CeBIL programme—grant no. NNF23SA0087056).

detail.abstract: Cryptographic algorithms do not remain secure indefinitely. Replacing one is rarely simple, since algorithms are embedded deep within the systems that rely on them, and systems that cannot update their cryptography become legacy liabilities. Cryptographic agility, the capacity to replace and adapt cryptographic algorithms whilst preserving security and ongoing operations, offers a response to this problem. Its most urgent driver is the quantum threat to public-key cryptography and the post-quantum migration now underway, though its significance is independent and enduring, extending to future cryptographic transitions. This article examines the concept of cryptographic agility within EU cybersecurity law. It argues that the regulatory framework is on a trajectory towards recognising agility as a general, operationalised requirement, and that this trajectory can be identified, assessed, and accelerated. No EU instrument expressly requires agility in its primary text, and the references that have appeared are patchwork and undefined. Across four principal instruments, the GDPR, NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act, and DORA, the article maps the pathways for embedding the concept, distinguishing those where Commission delegated and implementing regulations have already used agility language from those where the route runs through the 'state of the art', harmonised standards, or supervisory practice. It then contends that the EU can and should move to give the requirement determinate content on its own terms rather than awaiting its organic percolation into the 'state of the art'. As the means to do so largely exist within the current framework, doing so requires institutional action (including guidance, standardisation, and certification) rather than reform of the primary acquis.

title: The Sovereignty Stack - Engineering Integrity from Classical to Quantum AI

detail.title: The Sovereignty Stack - Engineering Integrity from Classical to Quantum AI
detail.abstract: The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence systems has introduced unprecedented sociotechnical risks, driven largely by the prioritization of short-term delivery velocity over long-term architectural stability. This paper is a theory-building and framework-development study that synthesizes evidence from software engineering, interpretable machine learning, and AI governance scholarship to advance two interconnected arguments. First, the prevailing velocityfirst development paradigm creates a compounding cycle of technical debt, algorithmic opacity, and proxy discrimination that reactive crisis management cannot address-a condition termed here the Velocity Trap. Second, and critically for the governance community, the classical AI governance frameworks currently being constructed are already obsolete: they are designed for a horse that has left the barn. Quantum AI is not a future contingency; it is an accelerating present, and its structural properties-superposition, entanglement, and measurement-induced collapse-render post-hoc explainability not merely unreliable but physically impossible as a governance instrument. To address both failures, this paper advances the Luevano Standard: a proposed adaptive, riskstratified governance framework grounded in the civil rights legacy of Luevano v. Campbell (1981) and the disparate impact doctrine of Griggs v. Duke Power Co. (1971). Because the Luevano Standard mandates inherent interpretability over post-hoc explanation, proactive architectural governance over reactive remediation, and regulated self-regulation over rigid mandate, it is structurally positioned to survive the classical-to-quantum transition. This paper introduces the Sovereign Stack as the technical instantiation of that standard-a layered architecture in which governance obligations are engineered into the foundation, not appended after deployment. The Luevano Standard is the saddle for the quantum horse. The question is whether the governance community will put it on before the horse accelerates beyond reach.

title: From Classical Coordination to Keynesian Uncertainty: Informational Distance and Institutional Possibilities Beyond Money and Interest

detail.title: From Classical Coordination to Keynesian Uncertainty: Informational Distance and Institutional Possibilities Beyond Money and Interest

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a theoretical/conceptual study and does not involve human subjects, patients, or participant data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper reinterprets the classical-Keynesian divide as a difference in informational regimes rather than as a simple opposition between competing universal theories. Classical coordination is understood as most applicable when coordination burdens remain manageable relative to society's capacity to process, verify, and coordinate relevant information. Keynesian uncertainty becomes dominant when informational distance is high: when coordination burdens exceed coordination capacities and economic agents rely more heavily on scalar mechanisms such as money, interest rates, prices, and aggregate indicators. The paper develops a simple framework in which informational distance is represented by the ratio of coordination burden to coordination capacity. Within this framework, money and interest are interpreted not as permanent primitives, but as historically contingent coordination mechanisms that bundle both fundamental and distance-induced functions. As informational distance declines, some functions historically delegated to money and interest may become less necessary as generalized scalar mechanisms and increasingly subject to institutional design. The argument does not predict the disappearance of money or interest, nor does it prescribe a particular institutional destination. Rather, it identifies conditions under which arrangements commonly treated as necessities may become matters of institutional choice.

title: Digital Access to German Civil Courts
affiliations: University of Bremen - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Digital Access to German Civil Courts
detail.abstract: The digitalisation of civil court access in Germany has been a decadeslong process marked by legislative ambition, structural inertia, and persistent implementation failures. This contribution traces the evolution of electronic legal communication, electronic case files, and video hearings from their statutory origins to the present day, with particular attention to the asymmetric outcome that has emerged: a professional-user infrastructure that is largely functional and a citizen-facing infrastructure that, despite the 2023 launch of MeinJustizPostfach, remains fragmentary-not least because of the structural asymmetry of consent to electronic service under § 173 ZPO. Against that backdrop, the contribution turns to the Act of 22 December 2025 on the Development and Piloting of an Online Procedure in Civil Jurisdiction-the most significant procedural reform in German civil litigation in many years. The Act introduces a new Book 12 to the Code of Civil Procedure. It establishes a digitally integrated, optional procedure before district courts for monetary claims up to €10,000, supported by guided digital input systems, a federal communication platform, structured data exchange, flexible digital evidence taking, and a reduced fee schedule. Situated within what Hess has described as the fourth wave of the access-to-justice movement, the procedure functions as the domestic counterpart to the European Small Claims Procedure. While the reform addresses several of the structural deficits that have impeded digitalisation in the past, it does not resolve them. Three problems persist: a pilot trap, in that the Act creates possibilities rather than rights and leaves rollout to state discretion; a federalism problem, in that the constitutional tension between federal rule-making and state-level implementation responsibility remains intact and federal funding remains a political agreement rather than a constitutional entitlement; and a user problem, in that the demand side of access to justice-whether ordinary citizens will find, understand, and use the new procedure-is left largely to chance. The very title of the Act, referring to 'Development and Piloting', signals that the legislature did not expect this to be the last word. The history of judicial digitalisation in Germany is, after all, a history of legislation that was not implemented, not funded, or not used. Whether the Online Procedure escapes that pattern is a question that only the next decade can answer.

title: Two Decades of Cybersecurity and IS Governance in Europe and Around the World: A Bibliometric Analysis with Implications for Strategic IT Management
affiliations: , University of Freiburg and Kiel University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: Two Decades of Cybersecurity and IS Governance in Europe and Around the World: A Bibliometric Analysis with Implications for Strategic IT Management
detail.abstract: Cybersecurity has become a strategic imperative for organizations and policymakers, yet the evolving research landscape that informs strategic IT and IS governance decisions remains poorly mapped. Through bibliometric analysis of 43,662 publications (2003-2022), we examine how cybersecurity research has evolved globally and in Europe across thematic priorities, geographic distribution, and citation impact. The field shifted from network security toward machine learning and cloud security, with governance and privacy gaining prominence after the Snowden revelations (2013) and GDPR (2018). European-focused research represents 27.5% of global output, yet grew nine-fold over the study period versus a five-fold global increase. Despite smaller scale, European-focused research achieves comparable citation impact at top performance levels, suggesting quality parity with global benchmarks. Our findings identify emerging thematic priorities, validate European-focused research as a competitive knowledge source, highlight geographic concentration patterns while informing strategic IT management and IS governance decisions at organizational and policy levels.

title: Toward a Platform State: NIK-Centric Identity Architecture as a Structural Solution to Fragmentation, Fiscal Leakage, and Service Inefficiency in Indonesia's Digital Governance Transition

detail.title: Toward a Platform State: NIK-Centric Identity Architecture as a Structural Solution to Fragmentation, Fiscal Leakage, and Service Inefficiency in Indonesia's Digital Governance Transition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a conceptual policy analysis based entirely on publicly available secondary literature and does not involve human participants, clinical trials, or private medical data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

keywords.keywords: digital identity infrastructure; governance interoperability; public service architecture; NIK; e-KTP; institutional fragmentation; digital state transformation; INA Digital; SPBE; Indonesia

detail.abstract:
Indonesia's public service architecture remains structurally fragmented, organized around competing sectoral identity systems that operate in administrative isolation. Citizens navigating state services must present separate credentials for healthcare enrollment, social assistance eligibility, fuel subsidy access, tax compliance, and electoral participation, a design that generates redundant data, chronic inclusion and exclusion errors, and substantial fiscal leakage. This paper argues that this fragmentation is not incidental but systemic, and that addressing it requires a foundational rethinking of how the state manages identity as a governance infrastructure.

The central proposition is that Indonesia's e-KTP, anchored by the Nomor Induk Kependudukan (NIK) as a universal primary key, constitutes an underutilized architecture capable of functioning as a unified national digital identity layer. Rather than treating e-KTP as a citizen identification document, this framework reconceptualizes it as core state infrastructure, a cross-sectoral interoperability mechanism integrating welfare distribution, healthcare systems, subsidy targeting, taxation, education financing, financial inclusion, and electoral administration within a single identity plane. Drawing on conceptual analysis, comparative governance evidence from Estonia's X-Road framework, India's Aadhaar-based digital public infrastructure, and Singapore's SingPass ecosystem, and empirical grounding from Indonesia's own NIK-DTKS matching experience and SATUSEHAT implementation, the paper develops a theoretical model for NIK-centric integration and examines its institutional preconditions. The analysis identifies measurable governance gains, including improved targeting accuracy, reduced administrative duplication, and diminished opportunities for benefit fraud, while foregrounding the constraints that have historically impeded integration: institutional ego, asymmetric data quality across agencies, interoperability deficits, and risks of state surveillance that any serious deployment must constitutionally bound. The paper concludes that Indonesia's digital governance reform hinges less on technological readiness than on political will and institutional design. Positioning e-KTP as platform state infrastructure reframes the NIK not as a number on a card, but as the connective tissue of a coherent, accountable digital state.

title: Bangladesh Tourist Spot Recommendation System Using Hybrid Machine Learning Techniques
affiliations: Dhaka International University

detail.title: Bangladesh Tourist Spot Recommendation System Using Hybrid Machine Learning Techniques

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no conflicts of interest regarding the publication of this paper. The research was conducted independently without any financial, commercial, or personal relationships that could have influenced the results or interpretation of the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, clinical data, or sensitive personal information. Therefore, formal ethics approval was not required. The research is based on publicly available data on tourist attractions in Bangladesh.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was conducted as an independent academic project.

detail.abstract:
Tourism plays a significant role in the economic and cultural development of a country. Bangladesh possesses a wide variety of tourist attractions, including historical sites, natural landscapes, beaches, waterfalls, religious places, and archaeological monuments. However, tourists often face difficulties in identifying suitable destinations due to the lack of intelligent recommendation systems specifically designed for Bangladesh. Existing tourism platforms mainly provide static information and do not offer personalized recommendations based on user preferences and geographical proximity. 
This research proposes a hybrid tourist spot recommendation system for Bangladesh that combines content-based filtering and location-based recommendation techniques. A structured dataset containing tourist attractions from different divisions of Bangladesh is utilized. The proposed system analyzes tourist spot categories, regional information, and geographical coordinates to generate personalized recommendations. Cosine Similarity is employed to identify attractions with similar characteristics, while the Haversine Distance formula is used to calculate geographical proximity between users and tourist destinations.
 The proposed framework aims to improve travel planning by providing accurate and personalized tourist recommendations. The system is implemented using Python, Pandas, Scikit-Learn, and Streamlit. Performance evaluation is conducted using standard recommendation metrics, including Precision, Recall, and F1-Score. The findings demonstrate that integrating user preferences with location-based information can significantly enhance recommendation quality and user satisfaction.
