declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human participants, human-subject data, patient data, animal subjects, or experimental interventions requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: In the current age digital information can be easily copied, transferred, analysed and stored indefinitely, hence the control of each individual over personal information becomes crucial. We propose a simple and elegant solution to the privacy versus usability dilemma, which simultaneously makes the individual the owner of their data and eventually lays the foundations for a new industry, Databanking. We discuss how every stakeholder wins from our proposal, situate it against existing proposals and partial implementations, and outline the challenges to implementing these ideas, requiring action from both regulators and entrepreneurs.

title: Trust as Capital: The Trust-to-Capital Conversion Framework for Raising Healthcare Technology Finance in Africa and the Global South

detail.title: Trust as Capital: The Trust-to-Capital Conversion Framework for Raising Healthcare Technology Finance in Africa and the Global South

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the Founder and Chief Operating Officer of Chestify AI Labs, which is discussed as an illustrative case study in this paper. This relationship is disclosed in the interest of transparency. The theoretical framework and analysis presented represent the author's independent scholarly work, and no external funding or third-party influence affected the research or its conclusions.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The research was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Sub-Saharan Africa carries approximately 25 per cent of the global disease burden but hosts fewer than three per cent of the world’s health workforce, generating a structural diagnostic deficit that neither sustained donor generosity nor conventional market mechanisms have resolved (World Health Organization, 2021). Against a backdrop of an annual healthcare financing gap estimated at USD 26 billion (World Health Organization, 2019), blended-finance mobilization in African health systems totals under USD 3 billion annually (Convergence, 2024), while digital health ventures on the continent attract less than one per cent of global healthtech investment. The explanation offered by the financing literature, that the gap reflects risk, is partial at best: capital in African healthcare markets is systematically overpriced relative to realized default experience, with a perception premium of 100 to 260 basis points above comparably rated peers in other markets (Moody’s Analytics, 2020; United Nations Development Programme, 2023).

This paper proposes an integrated capital-raising framework for healthcare technology ventures in Africa and the Global South, anchored in the Trust-to-Capital Conversion (TCC) Function; a formal mathematical expression of the mechanism by which verifiable clinical trust is converted into investable capital across a defined financing horizon. Drawing on a Diagnostic Resilience Finance Framework (DRF) operationalized through the case of a healthcare technology company in Africa. The paper argues that the movement from diagnostic scarcity to systemic resilience is an act of deliberate financial engineering, not of charity.

Numerical calibration of the TCC Function over a twelve-month horizon demonstrates that a severe Trust Tax suppressing the capital multiplier by 75 per cent destroys approximately USD 223,800 of convertible capital without altering a single clinical metric. This provides the first formal, falsifiable expression of the perception premium as a capital-conversion mechanism. The paper concludes with differentiated implications for investors and development-finance institutions, founders and innovators, and policymakers, arguing that the TCC framework enables accurate, trust-anchored assessment of healthtech ventures whose potential has been systematically underpriced by conventional evaluation methods. The framework reconceptualizes diagnostic scarcity as a mispriced-risk problem correctable through disciplined capital sequencing, rather than a charity problem demanding permanent concessional subsidy.

title: Data and Artificial Intelligence Governance in Tanzania: Building a Responsible, Secure, and Inclusive Digital Future

detail.title: Data and Artificial Intelligence Governance in Tanzania: Building a Responsible, Secure, and Inclusive Digital Future

keywords: Artificial Intelligence Governance; Data Protection; Cybersecurity; Digital Transformation; Tanzania; Responsible AI; Data Sovereignty

detail.abstract: Background: Tanzania’s digital landscape is evolving at a rapid pace. The ICT sector is no longer just an emerging field; it has become a primary driver of the economy and a catalyst for transforming public service delivery. As data-driven technologies and Artificial Intelligence (AI) become more prevalent, they offer immense potential for progress, yet they simultaneously present complex governance challenges. Research Problem: Despite significant strides—such as the enactment of the Personal Data Protection Act in 2022 and the ongoing development of a National AI Strategy—Tanzania lacks a cohesive, homegrown governance framework. Currently, data protection, cybersecurity, AI ethics, and inclusive development operate in isolation. Without a unified approach, the country remains vulnerable to risks such as data breaches, algorithmic bias, cyberattacks, and widening digital inequality. Methodology: This paper employs a qualitative methodology, centered on policy analysis and comparative case studies. It examines Tanzanian laws, policies, and regulatory institutions, comparing them against models from four key African nations: Kenya, Rwanda, South Africa, and Nigeria. Furthermore, it draws insights from global frameworks. The analysis is built upon a comprehensive review of government documents, legal statutes, regulatory guidelines, academic literature, and significant reports from international development organizations. Key Findings: Tanzania’s data governance is currently anchored by three primary pieces of legislation: the Cybercrimes Act (2015), the Electronic Transactions Act (2015), and the Personal Data Protection Act (2022). Since becoming operational in 2023, the Personal Data Protection Commission has made significant progress, registering over 14,000 institutions by April 2026. Additionally, the National AI Strategy is nearing completion following a UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment in 2025. However, substantial obstacles remain. Overlapping jurisdictions between different institutions often lead to regulatory friction, enforcement mechanisms remain inconsistent, and there is a notable shortage of specialized AI talent; for instance, only 20 individuals successfully entered Data and Artificial Intelligence Governance in Tanzania 3 advanced AI training in 2025 out of 214 applicants. The issue is compounded by the fact that African data is critically underrepresented in global AI development—contributing less than 4% of training data—which heightens the risk of biased algorithms. Digital inequality also persists, with smartphone penetration stagnating at 41.8%. Moreover, while 70% of CEOs express readiness for AI adoption, only 19% have made the necessary financial investments to support it. Recommendations: To move forward, Tanzania must adopt a multi-layered governance approach that integrates policy, regulation, technology, human capital, and social evolution. Essential steps include establishing a formal AI risk classification system, investing in local data infrastructure to ensure greater data sovereignty, and expanding AI education—potentially through the proposed National Institute for Digital and AI Technologies. Finally, the country must implement inclusive digital literacy programs to address the gender gap and bridge the divide between urban and rural populations. Original Contribution: This paper offers the first comprehensive academic examination of Tanzania's evolving data and AI governance landscape. It introduces a unique, five-layer governance framework specifically tailored to Tanzania’s specific legal, institutional, and socioeconomic context.

title: Judgment Cost Theory: The Accountable Bearing of Judgment in an Age of Cheap Prediction

detail.title: Judgment Cost Theory: The Accountable Bearing of Judgment in an Age of Cheap Prediction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence drives the marginal cost of prediction toward zero, the binding constraint on consequential action shifts from predicting outcomes to bearing the judgment that converts predictions into accountable decisions. This paper develops Judgment Cost Theory (JCT), which defines judgment cost as the burden of exercising accountable judgment under irreducible uncertainty-the joint product of accountability for outcomes and the non-programmable uncertainty under which decisions are made. The theory specifies a mechanism by which cheap prediction makes judgment, not prediction, the scarce and value-bearing input; derives organizational consequences (judgment intermediation and judgment governance); and states boundary conditions and a falsification criterion. Its most distinctive empirical claim is that judgment cost-not skill, routineness, or cognitive complexity-predicts which work resists automation. We test this claim in a retrospective study (Experiment 1) that constructs a Judgment Cost Index from O*NET occupational descriptors and relates it to nine independent measures of occupational AI exposure, controlling for cognitive complexity, routineness, education, and wage. Across eight of nine measures-including all five generative-AI-era indices-higher judgment cost predicts significantly lower AI exposure beyond the controls, with the largest effects for the newest measures; the index also predicts employment persistence (2016-2025), and the result survives an extensive robustness battery. The lone null is the field's known outlier measure. Findings support JCT's core proposition and locate judgment cost as a distinct, consequential, and measurable construct.

title: Estimating and Understanding Corporate GHG Emissions from Financial Statements
affiliations: , Vlerick Business School and KU Leuven - Faculty of Business and Economics (FEB)

detail.title: Estimating and Understanding Corporate GHG Emissions from Financial Statements
detail.abstract: We examine whether audited financial statements contain structured information about firms' operational Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions beyond what is captured by common industry × location intensity benchmarks. Using a global sample of listed firms from Compustat and FactSet and a deliberately constrained set of core financial statement line items, we estimate firm-specific emissions using a Gradient Boosting Machine. Relative to the strongest industry × location scaling benchmark, the accounting-based model reduces the out-of-time prediction error by approximately 37%. Explainability analyses show that the financials-emissions mapping is nonlinear, sector-contingent, and shaped by cost and asset structure rather than by firm scale alone. These findings challenge the proportionality assumption underlying common emissions-intensity ratios and suggest that financial statements contain useful signals about firms' operating configurations. We further construct derivative-based sensitivity measures based on Generalized Additive Models to summarize local associations between individual financial items and predicted emissions, providing diagnostic evidence on the heterogeneity underlying the benchmark improvement.

title: The Override Floor and the Consistency of the Audit Response Why Non-Identification Floors Control Reliance, Not Only Management Override

detail.title: The Override Floor and the Consistency of the Audit Response Why Non-Identification Floors Control Reliance, Not Only Management Override
detail.abstract: Risk-based auditing conditions the auditor's response on the assessed risk-except for management override of controls, where the standards require a response irrespective of any assessment. This paper reads that exception as a floor: a minimax response held across the range of a dependence the engagement cannot identify, rather than tuned to a point within it. The dependence in question-the correlation, on the misstatements the audit fails to catch, between control failure and substantive-procedure failure-is non-identified, and a response cannot be conditioned on a quantity that cannot be evaluated; the control credit that conditions on it is not reasonable assurance but a wager the audit market's cost structure biases downward. The same non-identification underwrites override and ordinary control failure alike, so the standards floor one source of dependence while crediting the others through an effectiveness testing blind to it. The floor is therefore too narrow: consistency requires its extension to control reliance at large, and no mechanism of disclosure can engineer the dependence away-the revelation route coincides with the region where the credit was already legitimate, rather than enlarging it. A Γ-minimax analysis locates the floor's height and the boundary of that region as functions of the loss asymmetry. The argument terminates in a result the standards furnish against themselves: at the intersection of universal override risk and the exhaustion of substantive evidence, no response guarantees bounded residual risk, and the probabilistic reading of reasonable assurance cannot be sustained. Where it fails, what remains is deterrence, not measurement.

title: Better Buildings, Better Scores? The Short-Run Effect of a Large School Construction Programme
affiliations: University of Glasgow

detail.title: Better Buildings, Better Scores? The Short-Run Effect of a Large School Construction Programme
detail.abstract: Causal evidence on the effect of school capital investment on education outcomes in the existing literature is scarce and mixed. This paper provides new evidence on this by studying the short-run effect of a large school construction programme in England. Taking advantage of the phasing design that the whole programme is delivered in a sequence of waves, I apply difference-indifferences techniques to elicit the causal effect of school capital investment on student academic achievement. I find that the programme disproportionately affects pupils from different backgrounds: academically and socioeconomically disadvantaged students enjoy large and positive test score gains, while their more advantaged counterparts do not. The overall effect remains positive but much smaller and insignificant. There is some evidence suggesting heterogeneous effects by school types, project types, and time lengths of building occupancy. I further demonstrate that these results are not driven by student selection into newly built schools.

title: Narrative Displacement and Intrinsic Value: A DCF and SOTP Analysis of the Spacex
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Narrative Displacement and Intrinsic Value: A DCF and SOTP Analysis of the Spacex
detail.abstract: This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the Initial Public Offering (IPO) of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX), examining the profound disconnect between its $2.23 trillion market valuation and its underlying operational and financial realities. By integrating Robert Shiller's theory of Narrative Economics (Shiller, 2019) and Charles Kindleberger's lifecycle of speculative manias (Kindleberger, 1978), the study deconstructs the "Musk Premium" and the strategic narrative shift catalyzed by the xAI merger. Utilizing a multi-stage Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model and a Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) valuation based on the May 2026 S-1 prospectus, the paper identifies a 164.83% speculative premium and predicts a severe market correction as the "Mania" phase transitions into "Distress" due to technical impediments and governance conflicts.

title: Parallel Dollar Premia and Inflation Forecasting: Evidence from Argentina

detail.title: Parallel Dollar Premia and Inflation Forecasting: Evidence from Argentina
detail.abstract: We ask whether a publicly observable parallel-market ("blue") dollar premium improves real-time inflation forecasts in a high-inflation economy, beyond the official exchange rate and standard controls. Using monthly Argentine data over 2017-2025 and recursive, expanding-window pseudo-out-of-sample evaluation, a forecasting model that adds the premium to a nested traditional pass-through model lowers mean squared prediction error for future inflation, with modest gains at short horizons and larger gains at long horizons. The augmented model beats stronger benchmarks too, including an AR(1) and a forecast combination, and the three-tosix-month gain survives excluding the 2023-2025 devaluation window, though we show transparently that much of the longest-horizon gain reflects the model tracking that episode rather than uniform accuracy, and we report where and when the gain accrues. As a diagnostic we also estimate the differential pass-through during high-premium states with local projections and an orthogonalised Double Machine Learning local projection: it is positive under OLS but does not survive flexible conditioning on global financial conditions including the US short rate, so we read the premium's value as predictive, not structural. The premium is a historical signal of dollarization pressure, closely related over the recent overlap to the pressure reflected in stablecoin markets; we use it as a proxy for that pressure, not a direct on-chain measure, and leave the crosscountry extension to future work.

title: MSTCN: A BOF Steelmaking Endpoint Temperature Prediction Method with Multi-scale Spatio-Temporal Complex Network
affiliations: University of Science and Technology Beijing, University of Science and Technology Beijing, University of Science and Technology Beijing, University of Science and Technology Beijing, University of Science and Technology Beijing, University of Science and Technology Beijing, University of Science and Technology Beijing and University of Science and Technology Beijing

detail.title: MSTCN: A BOF Steelmaking Endpoint Temperature Prediction Method with Multi-scale Spatio-Temporal Complex Network
detail.abstract: The converter steelmaking process is an important part of the steel industry. Accurate prediction of the endpoint temperature in basic oxygen furnace (BOF) steelmaking is crucial for ensuring molten steel quality and reducing resource consumption. However, the high dynamic, multi-scale, and multi-directional characteristics of furnace mouth flame textures pose significant challenges to existing feature extraction methods. To address these issues, this paper proposes a flame image texture feature extraction framework based on Multi-scale Spatio-Temporal Complex Network (MSTCN). The proposed method integrates Multi-scale Spatial Complex Network (MSCN) and Multi-scale Temporal Complex Network (MTCN) to simultaneously capture the spatial distribution patterns and dynamic evolution features of flame textures at multiple scales. Furthermore, traditional LBP-GLCM static features are incorporated to provide complementary texture descriptions. Specifically, vertices are generated through multi-scale patch partitioning and filtered via K-means clustering, Edges are established based on color, spatial, and temporal distances to construct the complex networks. Statistical features extracted from vertex degree distribution histograms of MSTCN. Then the features are concatenated with static features to form the flame texture descriptor, which is then fed into a Support Vector Regression (SVR) model for endpoint temperature prediction. Extensive experiments on a real-world steelmaking production line dataset demonstrate that MSTCN significantly outperforms the baseline methods. Meanwhile, ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each core module in the proposed framework.

title: The Role of Central Bank Leadership in Monetary Policy Effectiveness: Lessons from the Western Hemisphere
affiliations: University of Cambridge, University of Cambridge and University of Cambridge

detail.title: The Role of Central Bank Leadership in Monetary Policy Effectiveness: Lessons from the Western Hemisphere
detail.abstract: This study examines the extent to which central bank leadership affects monetary policy effectiveness in the Western Hemisphere. While existing literature has extensively analyzed the role of central bank independence, policy frameworks, and institutional credibility, the influence of leadership remains relatively underexplored. Using a qualitative comparative case study approach, the paper analyzes five economies; Chile, Jamaica, Barbados, Guyana, and Suriname, based on secondary data from central bank reports, IMF publications, and academic literature. The findings suggest that central bank leadership affects monetary policy effectiveness indirectly through four main channels: institutional credibility, policy communication, strategic decision-making, and organizational effectiveness. Countries with stronger leadership-related institutional characteristics tend to exhibit more stable inflation outcomes, stronger credibility, and improved macroeconomic performance. The results indicate that leadership acts as a complementary factor that reinforces, rather than replaces, formal monetary policy institutions. The study contributes to literature by integrating leadership theory with monetary economics and highlighting its relevance for monetary policy outcomes in small open economies.

title: Regulating Capital Market Abuses in Nigeria: The Role of the Securities and Exchange Commission
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Regulating Capital Market Abuses in Nigeria: The Role of the Securities and Exchange Commission
detail.abstract:
Economic development, which is one of the essential aspects in the growth and improvement of any society, it is associated with the enhancement of the standard of living, employment, and the general well-being of the people. Integral to this process are capital markets, which mobilize savings from individuals and institutions and channel them into long-term investment, thereby enabling investment and economic growth. At the heart of every functioning capital market is one key element; trust. The meaning of “trust” encompasses two related but meaningfully distinct concepts. The first, which is systemic or institutional trust, is the confidence of market participants in the market as a whole; its infrastructure, rules, and the credibility of its regulator. The second is informational trust, which is the confidence that prevailing prices reflect true value and no participant is trading on an informational advantage unavailable to others. Where these essentials are not carried out, capital market abuse comes in. Such practices weaken the public trust, discourage participation, erode or undermine investors’ confidence, and significantly impede economic growth.

Market abuse has been of great concern in the Nigerian capital; the role of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is critical in preserving the integrity of the capital market as well as the Nigerian economy at large, because a lapse in its ability to properly regulate the capital market will immediately, amongst other things, erode the confidence investors have in the financial system of the country, which in turn has the capacity to cause a lot of damage to the Nigerian economy. As a result, the SEC introduced rules and regulations, and the Investment and Securities Act (ISA 2025)was enacted to curb these abuses and hold offenders liable.

This paper aims to examine the adequacy of the provisions of the Investment and Securities Act (ISA) 2025, and the efficiency of the SEC in curbing market abuse vis-à-vis the challenges faced in the enforcement of regulations aimed at curbing market abuse in the Nigerian capital market. To achieve this, this paper attempts to examine the provisions of ISA 2025 on market abuses, it examines whether the SEC has lived up to its mandate in preventing market abuses in Nigeria and the challenges in the enforcement of market abuse regulation. The paper concludes by proffering solutions to addressing the challenges.

title: The Business of Quantum Technologies: Innovation Dynamics in the Energy Sector
affiliations: CGI Business Consulting, , Carnegie Mellon University - David A. Tepper School of Business, University of Cambridge and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Business of Quantum Technologies: Innovation Dynamics in the Energy Sector

contentType.other: Chapter in Digital Transformation in the Quantum Computing Age (Edited by Jay Liebowitz)

detail.abstract:
The global energy transition — from centralized fossil-fuel systems toward distributed, decarbonized electricity networks — is occurring precisely as quantum technologies cross the threshold from laboratory curiosity to early commercial deployment. This chapter examines the intersection of these two structural shifts, asking which quantum technologies are likely to matter for energy systems, how adoption trajectories depend on market archetype and institutional structure, and how quantum capabilities may ultimately reshape business models and industry architecture.

We develop an analytical framework that integrates the Multi-Level Perspective on sociotechnical transitions with a business model innovation lens organized around the "4Vs" — value proposition, value creation, value capture, and value network — applied across two market archetypes defined by the degree of electricity market liberalization and the scale of system actors. Vertically integrated markets (exemplified by France, China, and many municipal utility systems) offer coordination advantages and direct policy levers but risk institutional lock-in and slower niche experimentation. Liberalized or horizontally consolidated markets (exemplified by Great Britain, ERCOT, and the Nordic Pool architecture) lower barriers to entry and encourage innovation but face structural challenges in aligning incentives for system-wide quantum deployment.

Across all three pillars of quantum technology — sensing, communication, and computing — we find that quantum sensing is the most deployment-ready, with commercially available systems already applied to timing, magnetometry, and gravimetry; quantum communication occupies a middle tier with point-to-point QKD commercially available; and quantum computing, despite attracting the majority of investment and attention, remains at the prototype stage for energy-relevant applications. The post-quantum cryptographic migration is identified as the most time-sensitive near-term organizational priority.

We argue that quantum technologies should not be understood as isolated technical tools but as enabling components within wider sociotechnical transitions, whose adoption is mediated by political economy, regulatory architecture, and the three forms of incumbent lock-in — techno-economic, social and cognitive, and institutional and political. Near-term value is most likely to emerge through complementarities with existing digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence rather than wholesale technological substitution. For managers, this implies a strategic focus on capability development, experimentation, and partnership formation. For policymakers, the challenge is to design institutional arrangements that combine the coordination strengths of integrated systems with the innovation dynamism of liberalized markets, while ensuring equitable access to quantum resources does not become a new axis of competitive asymmetry.

The analysis is situated within the integrative POEM (Political Economy and Operations Management) framework, which recognizes that energy security — and hence quantum technology adoption in the energy sector — is fundamentally a global supply chain issue shaped by geopolitics, institutional structures, and the exercise of power, not logistics alone

title: Developing and Validating a Stakeholder-Based CSR Disclosure Assessment Framework for Chinese Listed Companies
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Developing and Validating a Stakeholder-Based CSR Disclosure Assessment Framework for Chinese Listed Companies
detail.abstract:
This study develops and validates a stakeholder-based framework for assessing corporate social responsibility (CSR) information disclosure among Chinese listed companies. Existing CSR and sustainability reporting frameworks, including international standards and reporting guidelines, are primarily designed from an organizational perspective and do not fully capture the distinctive responsibilities of listed companies as participants in capital markets. To address this gap, this study constructs a comprehensive CSR disclosure assessment framework that incorporates not only traditional stakeholder dimensions such as environmental, employee, market, and community responsibilities, but also investor responsibility and capital market responsibility.

The framework evaluates disclosure performance across multiple dimensions, including completeness, sufficiency, materiality, comparability, balance, readability, and disclosure willingness. It is applied to a hand-collected dataset covering CSR reports and corporate website disclosures of Chinese A-share listed companies from 2013 to 2015, representing more than 2,000 company-year observations. All disclosure information was manually collected, coded, and evaluated using a consistent methodology.

The empirical results demonstrate that the framework is capable of distinguishing disclosure quality across industries, regions, and market segments, while producing stable and consistent evaluation outcomes over multiple reporting cycles. The study contributes to the literature by providing a stakeholder-oriented measurement architecture for CSR disclosure assessment and offers practical implications for regulators, investors, sustainability practitioners, and researchers interested in corporate transparency and accountability.

title: Sovereign Debt Sustainability Under Global Monetary Tightening: A Risk-Governed Framework for Emerging-Market Resilience, Refinancing Risk, and Debt-Crisis Prevention
affiliations: Kanzi Business Consultation

detail.title: Sovereign Debt Sustainability Under Global Monetary Tightening: A Risk-Governed Framework for Emerging-Market Resilience, Refinancing Risk, and Debt-Crisis Prevention

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper develops a risk-governed framework for sovereign debt sustainability in emerging economies under global monetary tightening. The renewed high-interest-rate environment has changed the arithmetic and politics of public debt: higher effective interest rates increase debt-service burdens, tighter liquidity raises refinancing risk, exchange-rate depreciation increases the domestic-currency value of foreign-currency liabilities, and volatile capital flows can transform liquidity pressures into solvency concerns. Drawing on classic pre-2006 sovereign debt and international finance literature and current institutional evidence from the IMF, World Bank, OECD, BIS, and UNCTAD, the study argues that debt sustainability should be assessed as a dynamic risk system rather than as a single threshold of debt-to-GDP. Methodologically, the paper applies an integrative conceptual and policy-analysis approach. It synthesizes debt-overhang theory, reputational models of default, currency-crisis models, original-sin and currency-mismatch literature, fiscal sustainability tests, capital-flow volatility frameworks, and sovereign debt restructuring debates. The paper contributes a twelve-part analytical architecture, including a sovereign debt sustainability risk matrix, a debt-dynamics framework, a highinterest-rate transmission model, a sovereign refinancing risk matrix, an international reserves adequacy framework, and an emerging-market debt resilience index proposal. The central conclusion is that emerging economies need to move from reactive debt-crisis management toward forward-looking debt resilience governance. This requires credible fiscal anchors, longer maturity profiles, deeper localcurrency debt markets, transparent debt statistics, targeted reserve buffers, macroprudential safeguards, realistic primary-balance paths, growth-supporting fiscal reform, and earlier, more orderly restructuring when solvency is no longer credible.

title: Are Multifractal Dynamics of Electroencephalogram Signals from Multi Fractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MFDFA) A Novel Approach to Extract Cognitive Flexibility Markers of Strategy and Rule Guessing in Human Science? A Comparative Approach Between MFDFA And Classic Fast-Fourier Transform
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Are Multifractal Dynamics of Electroencephalogram Signals from Multi Fractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MFDFA) A Novel Approach to Extract Cognitive Flexibility Markers of Strategy and Rule Guessing in Human Science? A Comparative Approach Between MFDFA And Classic Fast-Fourier Transform

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The present study was approved by the internal review board of the University of Cardiff and all the participants gave written informed consent before participating.
declarations.funderStatement: The author's research was sponsored and supported by Lumiere Education.

detail.abstract: Cognitive flexibility-the ability to adapt strategies and infer new rules-is crucial for navigating dynamic environments. However, traditional Electroencephalogram analysis methods, which often assume linearly and stationarity, may miss important features of brain dynamics. This study leverages Multi Fractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MFDFA) to extract multifractal markers from EEG recordings and explore their connection with cognitive flexibility. For that purpose, this study used a dataset that contains 60 EEG recordings from a sleep study. Precisely, 20 participants had their brain activity recorded during sleep after a transitive inference task, after sleep for post-test and after a week for long-term comparison purpose. Data analysis, EEG pre-processing, behavioural statistics and MFDFA were performed using Python. The present research aims to explore the potential of multifractal dynamics in EEG signals as a novel approach to extract cognitive flexibility markers of strategy and rule guessing in human science using Multi Fractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MFDFA).

title: Systemic Wellbeing and the Multi-node Stability Function: A Development Economics Model for Social, Ecological, and Institutional Stability

detail.title: Systemic Wellbeing and the Multi-node Stability Function: A Development Economics Model for Social, Ecological, and Institutional Stability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial, institutional, or personal conflicts of interest related to the research, writing, or dissemination of this manuscript. The work is produced independently as part of the author’s sovereign scholarly practice under TC Press.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified development-economics framework based on a Multi-Node Stability Function (MNSF), a mathematical model in which social, ecological, and institutional wellbeing are treated as interdependent components of a single systemic health condition. The model challenges the dominant individual-centric and GDP-centric paradigms by demonstrating that development outcomes depend on the minimum health of all critical nodes, not the average performance of isolated sectors. Drawing on the Oromo concept of nagaa-an indigenous systems-health logic in which personal wellbeing is inseparable from the wellbeing of family, community, animals, land, and the wider environment-the paper illustrates how pre-scientific societies encoded interdependence as a daily governance mechanism. The MNSF formalises this logic using weakest-link dynamics, entropy minimisation, and threshold-based stability conditions. Divergence from systemic wellbeing is shown to generate social inequality, ecological degradation, and institutional entropy. The paper extends the model to the context of autonomous civilisation, arguing that modern intelligence systems enable humanity to operationalise interdependence at planetary scale. Integrating indigenous systems logic with complexity science provides a viable foundation for sustainable development in the twenty-first century and beyond.

title: Weak Error Analysis of τ -Leaping Inference for Discrete Spatial Diffusion
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Weak Error Analysis of τ -Leaping Inference for Discrete Spatial Diffusion

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Work was funded by a multi-university research grant from Upenn and USC

detail.abstract: Discrete Spatial Diffusion (DSD) is a generative modeling framework that enforces exact conservation of discrete particle counts through a continuous-time, discrete-state Markov jump process on a spatial lattice. Inference in DSD is performed via binomial τ-leaping: a fixed-step discretization of the reverse-time jump process governed by a CFL step-size condition. Despite empirical success, the approximation error introduced by τ-leaping has not been characterized theoretically. In this paper we develop a rigorous weak error analysis for binomial τ-leaping applied to the DSD reverse process. We prove that, under regularity assumptions on the learned rate network and the forward-process transition semigroup, the total variation distance between the law of the true reverse-time process and that of the τ-leaping approximation at the terminal time is of order O(ε), where ε is the CFL tolerance. We further establish an explicit dimension-dependent constant governing this bound, and discuss implications for adaptive step-size selection and the number of function evaluations required during inference.

title: Judge Hacking in Recursive Debate Protocols: A Call for Solutions
affiliations: , Helmholtz Munich and Helmholtz Munich

detail.title: Judge Hacking in Recursive Debate Protocols: A Call for Solutions
detail.abstract: The debate protocol is a promising solution to the problem of supervising systems that are more capable than their supervisors, known as scalable oversight. It is proposed not only as an inferencetime procedure for adjudicating individual claims, but as a training protocol: the judge's verdict propagates back through the debate as a reward signal used to optimise the debaters. The judge here can be a human or some proxy for human feedback. Under idealised assumptions, debate incentivises truthfulness: the truthful claim is the uniquely optimal one to defend. Real judges, however, make systematic errors. Human judges exhibit predictable cognitive and domain-specific biases, and AI proxies exhibit predictable hallucinations and distributional failures. We argue that when these leaf-level errors are systematic and learnable, a dishonest debater can sometimes win debates while defending a falsehood or attacking truth by strategically steering the debate towards the judge's blind spots. We call this judge hacking. We ground this intuition in a formal game-theoretic model over recursive debate decomposition trees, where judge hacking occurs when the value of a false claim exceeds that of the corresponding true claim, and we speculate that the same mechanism plausibly arises across other variants of debate such as cross-examination and prover-estimator. The risk is most acute when debate is used for training because it introduces strong optimisation pressure to exploit the judge when it is valuable to do so. If debate is to be a viable oversight strategy, judge hacking must be mitigated. We study juries-panels of multiple judges-as a general, judge-side mitigation in need of empirical research. Independent, diverse juries can suppress idiosyncratic errors through a wisdom-of-the-crowd effect, but correlated or homogeneous juries can amplify shared systematic biases. We identify the maximum shared false-positive and false-negative bias over adversarially reachable leaves, together with the correlation structure of juror errors, as the key parameters governing jury robustness. We conclude with a call for urgent empirical and theoretical work on jury design for debate.

title: Does bank credit reach the firms that use it most productively? Banking Deregulation and the Reallocation of R&D
affiliations: University of Arizona - Department of Finance

detail.title: Does bank credit reach the firms that use it most productively? Banking Deregulation and the Reallocation of R&D
detail.abstract: I show that the entry of competition into local credit markets reallocates research and development toward the firms that use it most productively. Using the staggered removal of intrastate bank branching restrictions across U.S. states and a marginal revenue product framework, I find that deregulation raised the R\&D of high-return firms by roughly 40 percent relative to low-return firms in the same state, while leaving the total unchanged. In addition, firms with misallocated physical capital respond by raising leverage and physical investment, while the R\&D response operates through a pass through of internal funds to research. The reallocation is largest in states where banking is most concentrated before deregulation, pointing to the entry of competition as the operative channel. Finally, I document that this reallocation produces a measurable gain in aggregate productivity.

title: The Limits of Auctions under Ex-Ante Collusion
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics, Stanford University and Stanford University - Stanford University, Students

detail.title: The Limits of Auctions under Ex-Ante Collusion
detail.abstract: We study revenue-maximizing auction design when bidders can collude ex ante—i.e., before each bidder learns his value or decides whether to participate in the auction.  We show that bidders' ex-post private information about values does not preclude them from colluding efficiently, and as a result, the seller cannot guarantee a higher expected revenue than from posting an optimal price and rationing the good.  However, a posted-price mechanism leaves the seller vulnerable to inefficient collusion.  We construct mechanisms that guarantee the non-collusive expected revenue of an optimal posted price against a broad range of forms of ex-ante collusion—including collusion by rings comprised of subsets of bidders, rings that can commit to punish bidders who refuse to join, and rings of which some bidders may be unaware.  We show that achieving such a guarantee requires protecting bidders' ex-ante expected utilities against all such forms of collusion—a property that we term strong collusion-robustness.  With symmetric bidders, our strongly collusion-robust mechanism simply combines a posted price with a first-price knockout auction conducted by the seller on behalf of the bidders.

title: Anticipation and the Value of Social Insurance: Theory and Evidence from Survivor Benefits

detail.title: Anticipation and the Value of Social Insurance: Theory and Evidence from Survivor Benefits
detail.abstract: A large literature infers the value of social insurance using unanticipated benefit variation that is orthogonal to how households enter the insured state. These empirical designs deliver internal credibility, but evaluate social insurance in a setting where households cannot selfinsure before the shock. This paper argues that this feature inflates the estimated value of social insurance. I study this question in survivor insurance, where a recent literature reads the consumption-smoothing value of benefits off a labor-supply sufficient statistic, the causal effect of benefits on surviving spouses' post-widowhood earnings. I derive a correction linking that statistic to its welfare-relevant counterpart under a permanent regime: the latter equals the restricted-design estimate deflated by the share of the benefit change offset through nonlabor resources at widowhood. Two quasi-experimental designs within the same Swedish institutional setting bracket the extremes: the propensity to earn out of survivor benefits is a precisely estimated zero when the benefit cut is announced 22 years before widowhood and about-1 when benefit variation is realized at widowhood, indicating both low and high value of social insurance. Consistent with pre-shock self-insurance, households at high financial risk of widowhood raise their saving rate by 1.6 percentage points in response to a benefit cut announced decades before expected widowhood. Welfare evaluations built on unanticipated benefit variation therefore likely overstate the consumption-smoothing value of a permanent program change, when households self insure before the shock.

title: Cost-Effective Somewhere, Decision-Relevant Everywhere? A Global Systematic Review of Economic Evidence for Newer Type 2 Diabetes Therapies
affiliations: University of Otago, Curtin University, University of Otago and University of Otago

detail.title: Cost-Effective Somewhere, Decision-Relevant Everywhere? A Global Systematic Review of Economic Evidence for Newer Type 2 Diabetes Therapies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Background: Health systems facing rising type 2 diabetes burden and affordability constraints increasingly need locally relevant evidence to guide coverage of newer therapies. We assessed whether the global long-term economic evidence base is representative of disease burden, transferable across health systems, and relevant to equitable access.

Methods: We systematically reviewed long-term, model-based cost-effectiveness evaluations of newer glucose-lowering and cardiorenal–metabolic therapies for type 2 diabetes, searching six databases to Oct 31, 2025. Two reviewers screened, extracted data, and assessed quality and risk of bias. Descriptive analyses examined geography, disease-burden alignment, post-guideline evidence, transferability, and equity reporting. Incremental cost-effectiveness analysis-based comparisons were analysed using Poisson generalised estimating equation models, clustered by study and adjusted for funding, income setting, therapy category, and publication year. PROSPERO: CRD420251029741.

Findings: Of 1,488 records identified, 113 studies from 26 countries yielded 258 comparisons. 107 studies (95%) were from the WHO European, Western Pacific, or Americas regions. Among 112 single-country studies, 90 (80%) were from high-income and 22 (20%) from upper-middle-income settings; none represented lower-middle-income or low-income settings. High-income settings comprised 80% of studies but 18% of global type 2 diabetes disability-adjusted life-years. Favourable classifications were more frequent in high-income than upper-middle-income settings (93% vs 60%), but attenuated after adjustment (RR 1·10, 95% CI 0·87–1·39). Industry funding was not clearly associated with favourable classification after adjustment (RR 1·18, 95% CI 0·94–1·47). Identical-pair comparisons indicated context-dependent transferability. None used equity-sensitive methods.

Interpretation: Long-term economic evidence remains globally unrepresentative, conditionally transferable, and not equity-sensitive, leaving decisions least informed where affordability constraints and access inequities are greatest.

title: Stochastic Properties of Private Equity Returns Under the DARC Framework

detail.title: Stochastic Properties of Private Equity Returns Under the DARC Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded

detail.abstract: This paper demonstrates that the excess log return of private equity buyout funds over a public market benchmark exhibits the three properties required for stochastic modelling: a bounded mean, mean-reverting dynamics, and declining variance with fund maturity. We show that these properties are conditional on measuring returns under the Duration-Adjusted Return on Capital (DARC) framework with notional preservation-a condition that is not satisfied by conventional metrics such as IRR or TVPI. The analysis is conducted on a dataset of US and European buyout funds spanning 1995 to 2020, using real risk-free rates by date. A formal out-of-sample test confirms that the structural form of the stochastic process is stable across market regimes, while the long-run mean shifts with the public market cycle-a property we term regime dependence. The practical implication is a framework for constructing forward distributions of private equity returns conditional on an explicit public market scenario, with direct applications to secondary market pricing, portfolio stress testing, and LP performance attribution.

title: How Valuable Is Liquidity in Private Retirement Plans? Evidence From Increases in the Minimum Access Age
affiliations: University of Melbourne, University of Melbourne - Faculty of Business and Economics, Melbourne Institute: Applied Economic & Social Research, Deakin University, Deakin University - Deakin Business School,  and Government of the Commonwealth of Australia - Australian Tax Office

detail.title: How Valuable Is Liquidity in Private Retirement Plans? Evidence From Increases in the Minimum Access Age
detail.abstract: A key design issue for private retirement plans is their liquidity before retirement age. We estimate the effects of an Australian policy reform that reduced private pension liquidity through increases in the minimum access age by birthdate. Using administrative data and a regression discontinuity design, we find small reductions in withdrawals, no employment response and reductions in contributions that point to early access being a valuable source of precautionary liquidity, especially for financially engaged individuals. Overall, as reductions in contributions largely offset the savings from reduced withdrawals, increases in the access age have little effect on net private pension savings.

title: Alpha-TDG: Technology-Driven Growth as a New Dimension of Capital-Market Signals

detail.title: Alpha-TDG: Technology-Driven Growth as a New Dimension of Capital-Market Signals

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The opinions expressed herein belong solely to the author and do not represent any current or past institutional affiliations.
declarations.funderStatement: No founder

detail.abstract: Capital-market signals have evolved through two generations-passive market-capitalization weighting (how to allocate) and ESG screening (whether to hold). Neither addresses a question increasingly central to longhorizon firm value in the age of general-purpose artificial intelligence: which firms capture the surplus of a new general-purpose technology (GPT), at what stage of the cycle, and through which mechanism. We propose Alpha-TDG (Technology-Driven Growth) as a new dimension, operationalized through two paired indices. On the demand side, the Hedge Resilience Index (HRI) is a firm-quarter composite of seven equallyweighted, normalized indicators aggregated under a single universal formula; it maps to a five-position Ucurve and is decomposed post hoc into five firm-level paradigms together with an AI Revenue Taxonomy Standard (ARTS) classifying AI revenue into three auditable tiers. On the supply side, the AI Supply-Chain Index (ASCI) characterizes the structural state of the AI ecosystem across five vertical layers and six structural indicators per layer, mapping to an inverted-U regime curve from acute tightness to glut. The two indices are joined through four channels-a cycle-stage deflator for capital-intensive infrastructure firms, an aggregate AI-washing consistency check, a tactical ETF tilt, and a joint two-dimensional map. We accompany the framework with a contemporary cross-sectional analysis of leading US-listed firms with material AI activity and, as the primary empirical contribution, a pre-registered confirmatory test design on a 50-firm US technology, media, and telecommunications (TMT) quarterly panel (2021-2025) with fully specified estimating equations and accept/reject rules for four falsifiable hypotheses (H1-H4). A code-based credibility architecture (open kernel, proprietary calibration) forecloses the measurement-divergence pathway documented in the ESG-ratings literature. We propose the framework rather than declare it validated; the open-source kernel is the explicit mechanism by which we invite validation.

title: Scholar-Practitioner Model for Wealth Management: An AI-Supported Cross-Cultural Framework for International RIA
affiliations: Bar-Ilan University

detail.title: Scholar-Practitioner Model for Wealth Management: An AI-Supported Cross-Cultural Framework for International RIA

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not Applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not Applicable

detail.abstract: The international expansion of Western Registered Investment Advisor (RIA) wealth management firms into culturally distant markets presents significant staffing and cross-cultural management challenges. This paper develops a comprehensive scholar-practitioner theoretical framework for geocentric staffing strategies grounded in classical cultural theories. Drawing on Hofstede's cultural dimensions, Hall's highcontext versus low-context communication framework, and the indigenous Chinese concept of mianzi (face), we propose a geocentric staffing model combining expatriate leadership with hostcountry national analysts. The framework is further informed by institutional theory, legitimacy theory, ethical relativism versus universalism, upper echelons theory, and agency theory. We identify four cross-cultural communication problems rooted in theoretical gaps between American and Chinese norms: direct versus indirect feedback, reluctance to ask questions, hierarchy in decision-making, and high-context versus low-context misunderstandings, deriving theory-grounded solutions for each. Leadership implications are examined through cultural intelligence and adaptive leadership, emphasizing Critical Interactional Competence. We articulate a novel role for AI as a theoryapplication aid-not a replacement for cultural competence-for consistently applying classical theories in daily operations. Drawing on empirical findings that even advanced AI systems exhibit limited cultural alignment, we argue AI serves as a practical aid, not a substitute for human judgment. The paper also addresses cross-cultural negotiation dynamics, corporate social responsibility, and ethics in international contexts. This scholarpractitioner approach bridges theory and practice, offering an integrated framework demonstrating how institutional pressures, legitimacy concerns, ethical considerations, cultural dimensions, leadership characteristics, and incentive structures collectively shape successful international expansion strategies for wealth management firms entering China.

title: Demand Composition and Corporate Credit Risk

detail.title: Demand Composition and Corporate Credit Risk
detail.abstract: Every business is outfitted for a particular composition of demand, the way an airline divides its cabin in proportion to the spending power it expects to board. When that composition shifts, revenue is lost even if total demand never falls, and the loss is invisible to the standard instruments: aggregates average it away, and the Gini watches income before debt service. This paper reduces a firm's exposure to such shifts to a single number, the breach threshold: the smallest cut in its customers' spending that would break its loan covenants. The threshold is set by three observable features of the business: how much of its revenue comes from the households losing spending power, how violently its cost structure converts lost revenue into lost profit, and how much headroom its financing leaves. Calibrated with published parameters, the threshold reproduces the ordering of Australia's record 2022-25 insolvency wave, which concentrated in the mid-market services whose customers had been squeezed, and is bound to an empirical design that can reject it. The claim is narrow: a firm's position on the spending distribution is credit information.

title: Consumable but Not Identifiable Longitudinally: A Matched Audit of ESG Narrative Change in Japanese Listed Firms

detail.title: Consumable but Not Identifiable Longitudinally: A Matched Audit of ESG Narrative Change in Japanese Listed Firms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an extensive user of Anthropic's Claude models for research and operational tasks, and Anthropic's claude-opus-4-7 is one of four models in the scoring ensemble used in this study; the author therefore declares awareness of a potential conflict of interest in this multi-provider comparison. To mitigate this, no systematic advantage was extended to any single provider in retry decisions or result retention, aggregation across providers was unweighted, and reasoning was disabled in all providers. Generative AI tools were used for language editing and document assembly only; all research design, data analysis, interpretation, and conclusions are the author's own. The author has no other financial or personal relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study analyzes publicly available corporate sustainability and financial disclosures of listed companies and does not involve human participants, patients, personal data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently. No institutional, governmental, or commercial funding was received.

detail.abstract: This data note examines whether ESG narrative disclosures that are machine-consumable at a single point in time remain longitudinally identifiable-that is, whether year-over-year changes in narrative scoring can be reliably computed and interpreted under a fixed extraction and scoring protocol. We apply the disclosure-based v3.1 four-model consensus scoring system (claude-opus-4-7 / gpt-5.5 / gemini-3.1-pro-preview / deepseek-v4-pro) to a 30-firm matched panel of Japanese Prime Market companies across three reporting years (FY2022, FY2023, FY2024). Of 60 targeted prior-year firm-year cells, 29 (48%) achieved full comparability (class A: distinct artifact, ≥10 extractable spans); 31 (52%) were classified as non-comparable (class C) due to late-stage sample replacement, document unavailability, CMS-induced artifact duplication, or CDN-blocked download. Restricting analysis to class-A prior-year cells, we compute 87 axis-year ΔN observations across 15 firms and identify 5 symmetric pair-year observations where both the SBTi-anchor and matched non-SBTi firm in the same pair achieved class-A comparability. Of the 87 ΔN rows, 63 (72.4%) are stable within the inter-model dispersion threshold. Among the 24 changing rows, 16 show positive ΔN coinciding with Japan's mandatory disclosure expansion (2022-2025), classified as E-regulation-aligned candidates. Critically, the dominant source of class-C classification is sample construction timing-16 of 31 class-C prior-year cells (all in Group B) are attributable to nine replacement firms whose prior-year PDFs were not in the acquisition inventory. This is a procedural asymmetry, not a finding about firm disclosure behavior. These findings constitute the third empirical proposition in a systematization of ESG disclosure accessibility: narrative comparability does not imply longitudinal identifiability.

detail.abstract:
Background: Palbociclib plus endocrine therapy improved progression-free survival (PFS) versus endocrine therapy alone in patients with endocrine-sensitive and endocrine-resistant disease (PALOMA-2 and 3). Whether the PFS benefit observed in PALOMA-2 and PALOMA-3 translates into a comparable real-world PFS (rwPFS) advantage, and how real-world evidence (RWE) compares with randomised controlled trial (RCT) estimates in the absence of concurrent control arms, remains an open methodological question.

Methods: We compiled RWE data from 16 published studies (n ≈ 11,500 patients; 2018–2025; ten countries/regions, including two multi-country European cohorts). Using a digital twin approach, parametric survival models were calibrated to reconstruct PFS curves for each data source. A digital comparator representing aromatase inhibitor (AI) monotherapy was constructed as a weighted composite of three independent sources: PALOMA-2 letrozole control arm (40%), P-REALITY X AI-alone cohort (35%), and MONALEESA-2 letrozole control arm (25%). Monte Carlo simulation (n = 500) quantified parametric uncertainty, and six alternative weighting scenarios tested robustness.

Findings: Pooled RWE 1L palbociclib plus AI median PFS was 22.8 months (range 15.1–36.7 months; −8.1% vs PALOMA-2). The digital comparator-derived HR was 0.62 (90% credible interval [CrI]: 0.52–0.74), bracketed by PALOMA-2 (HR 0.58) and P-REALITY X (HR 0.70), and stable across all six weighting scenarios (range: 0.616–0.632). RWE variability was attributable to line-of-therapy heterogeneity, follow-up maturity, and menopausal status distribution.

Interpretation: Palbociclib real-world effectiveness is consistent with RCT data, with modest and methodologically explicable attenuation (~8%). The digital twin framework provides a robust, reproducible tool for generating counterfactual comparators where concurrent control arms are unavailable, with direct applicability to all CDK4/6 inhibitors.

title: Does Fiscal Policy Shape Gender Equity? An Analysis of Infrastructure Investments
affiliations: University of Bristol

detail.title: Does Fiscal Policy Shape Gender Equity? An Analysis of Infrastructure Investments
detail.abstract: Employing a dynamic factor and common correlated effects modelling strategy, this paper investigates how the composition of public expenditure shapes the gendered dimensions of well-being across a panel of high-, middle-and low-income economies. To do this, we construct latent measures of women's capabilities, livelihoods and empowerment, grounded in the frameworks of Sen (1999) and Kabeer (1999), and examine the directional effects of government expenditure on social versus physical infrastructure on each dimension, before tracing the pathways between them through a structural equation framework. We find that, overall, women's well-being outcomes are more favourably responsive to public spending in the social sector, though the strength of this relationship varies systematically across income contexts. From our findings we are also able to draw some policy conclusions that speak to the role of public spending in advancing gender equality, and to the need for gender mainstreaming at the policy-making level.

title: The Funding Carry and a Cross-Venue Spread on Perpetual Futures: A Significance-Tested Study of Hyperliquid and Centralized Venues

detail.title: The Funding Carry and a Cross-Venue Spread on Perpetual Futures: A Significance-Tested Study of Hyperliquid and Centralized Venues
detail.abstract: Hyperliquid has rapidly become the dominant decentralized venue for perpetual futures (over US$6 billion in total value locked as of June 17, 2026), making the economics of its distinctive hourly funding mechanism increasingly consequential. Our central finding is a robust, economically sensible edge: Hyperliquid's funding structurally exceeds that of major centralized venues (Binance and Bybit, both over the full three-year sample) on the same assets by roughly 7% annualized (14.7% in 2024, 4.6% in 2025)-a delta-neutral cross-venue dislocation (long the centralized-venue perpetual, short the Hyperliquid perpetual) that is highly significant (Newey-West HAC t = 4-8), walk-forward consistent (4-5 of 5 folds), survives the cross-venue basis, capital, and transaction costs when held staticallyreturning roughly 7-11% on deployed capital at a prudent 2-3× per-leg leverage, with negligible liquidation risk-and, unlike the single-venue premium, remains statistically significant into 2026. The single-venue carry-long spot, short the perpetual-is a general phenomenon, present on every venue but far richer on Hyperliquid: a genuine, highly timevarying risk premium of ∼7% over the risk-free rate on Hyperliquid (17.9% in 2024, 3.6% in 2025) versus only ∼2-3% on Binance and Bybit-on notional, or ∼5% on the capital actually deployed at a prudent 2-3× short-leg leverage (Hyperliquid perps are USDC-margined). The methodology is validated by HAC paired t-tests, a block bootstrap, five-fold walk-forward, and a Deflated Sharpe that corrects for multiple testing; returns are measured in excess of the riskfree rate (the 3-month T-bill, which the on-chain Aave USDC supply rate tracks closely); and a factor-model alpha. We further test a battery of "smart" refinements-cost-recovery exits, cross-sectional allocation, ML return-tilts and tail-risk leverage, and options tailhedging-and all fail to beat a naive baseline, several significantly. We report these nulls as a feature: a cautionary catalog of holdout-selection artifacts that only out-of-sample, multiple-testing-corrected inference exposes.

title: The Declining Role of Deposits in Credit Creation
affiliations: Stanford University and

detail.title: The Declining Role of Deposits in Credit Creation
detail.abstract: Does deposit funding still drive credit creation? Deposit inflows affect credit directly, through banks' balance sheet response, and indirectly, through a feedback loop in which credit generates new deposits. Using exogenous deposit shocks and a structural model, we show that the total bank-credit impact of a $1 deposit inflow has fallen from $2.13 to $0.88 over two decades. Both channels have weakened: banks extend less credit out of each marginal deposit, reflecting greater costs of balance sheet expansion, and fewer credit proceeds recycle into stable deposits, consistent with declining deposit specialness and a greater use of non-bank alternatives. Central bank policy also matters: Quantitative Easing lowers the credit impact of a marginal deposit through higher capital costs, while Quantitative Tightening can raise it through scarcer liquidity. We show that non-bank credit is unlikely to offset the decline. These findings point to an implicit narrowing of banking that dampens credit creation and reshapes monetary and fiscal policy transmission.

title: Social Media Sentiment as a Leading Indicator of In-Store Product Demand: An Empirical Analysis

detail.title: Social Media Sentiment as a Leading Indicator of In-Store Product Demand: An Empirical Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Two pending patents (DSFE-2026-001, STRP-2026-002)
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Conventional retail demand forecasting systems rely predominantly on historical point-ofsale (POS) transaction data, which creates an inherent temporal lag that prevents retailers from responding to emergent consumer demand signals before they materialise in sales data. This paper investigates whether real-time social media sentiment constitutes a statistically significant leading indicator of in-store product demand across retail product categories. Employing a simulation-based empirical design, this study generates 1,680 hourly observations spanning 14 days across five product categories with distinct sentiment trajectories-viral positive, plateauing, complaint spiral, recall event, and stable positive. Aspect-based sentiment scores (SDDS) are computed using the VADER lexical model and correlated with simulated POS demand series using cross-correlation analysis, ordinary least squares regression with lagged predictors, and Granger causality tests. Results indicate that social media sentiment Granger-causes retail demand for all five product categories (p<0.0001), with an average optimal predictive lead time of 6.8 hours (range: 3-10 hours). Asymmetric effects are confirmed for products experiencing negative sentiment trajectories, with statistically significant demand suppression preceding observable POS decline by 4-10 hours (p<0.05). These findings have direct implications for retail inventory management, suggesting that social media sentiment signals can provide a viable, sub-daily forward indicator of store-level demand changes in both positive and negative directions.

title: Demand Forecasting Failures in Fast Fashion Supply Chains: A Comparative Analysis of Inventory Mismanagement and Overproduction Using Public Financial Disclosures

detail.abstract: Fast fashion retailers compete on speed: the ability to move a trend from runway to rack in weeks rather than months. This business model depends on accurate, fast-cycle demand forecasting, yet forecasting failures remain endemic to the sector and routinely surface in public financial disclosures as inventory write-downs, markdown costs, and impairment charges. This paper examines demand forecasting performance across three publicly traded fast fashion companies-Inditex (parent of Zara), H&M Group, and Boohoo Group (rebranded Debenhams Group in 2025)-using inventory metrics, markdown disclosures, and management commentary drawn from 10-K equivalent annual reports, interim financial statements, and earnings call transcripts published between 2024 and 2026. The analysis finds that forecasting outcomes diverge sharply based on three identifiable business analysis practices: the tightness of the design-to-shelf cycle, the discipline of inventory governance (open-to-buy management and markdown cadence), and the degree to which demand signals from point-of-sale data are fed back into near-term production decisions. Inditex's integrated, short-lead-time model produced consistently low and high-quality inventory levels. H&M showed measurable improvement in inventory productivity following a multi-year operational correction. Boohoo/Debenhams, by contrast, disclosed a £40 million write-down on surplus stock and a 65 percent reduction in inventory as part of an emergency pivot to a stock-lite marketplace model-a structural admission that its forecasting and buying processes had failed at scale. The paper concludes that demand forecasting failure in fast fashion is less a data science problem than a business analysis and governance problem, and proposes a framework business analysts can use to diagnose forecast-to-actual gaps before they surface as writedowns.

title: Measuring the Frontier: How Figures of Merit Shape Innovation
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), Anderson School of Management, Students

detail.title: Measuring the Frontier: How Figures of Merit Shape Innovation
detail.abstract: When a scientific or technical community confronts a new problem, it tends toward a shared figure of merit, such as a benchmark score, performance proxy, or model-evaluation task, so that scattered inventors can compare ideas and search the problem together. This paper argues that such a metric is a shared search representation: a simplification device for a problem landscape that no one can see whole. Yet because the communities that build these measures run on a currency of recognition, a metric that makes the innovation process comparable is also the channel through which attention and status flow. As a result, the coupling of metric to reward arises on its own, before any principal or third party decides that it should, because legibility is the reward channel. Over time, the representation can stop being what the community relies on to search with, instead serving as the target that it searches for. Furthermore, the metric can become embedded as a field paradigm, turning a subjective construct into a seemingly objective dimension of progress. Unlike metrics used in social settings, even if the community is not gaming the metric, the honest optimization of this proxy can narrow a field’s collective search, foreclosing the other directions that are not captured. I develop the mechanisms through which this occurs and illustrate them with the LINPACK benchmark. Taken together, because innovation communities largely run on recognition, the figure of merit that a field uses to explore the frontier ends up shaping where the frontier goes.

detail.abstract: This book traces the development of the fashion industry, providing insight into the business and, in particular, its interrelations with copyright law. The book explores how the greatest haute couture fashion designers also had a sense for business and that their attention to copyright was one of the weapons in protecting their market position. The work also confronts the peculiarities of the fashion industry as a means of demonstrating the importance of intellectual property protection while pointing out the many challenges involved. A central aim is to provide a copyrightability test for fashion goods based on detailed analysis of the legal regulations in the USA and EU countries, specifically Italy, France, the Netherlands, Germany and Poland. The book will be of interest to researchers and academics working in the areas of Intellectual Property Law, Copyright Law, Business Law, Fashion Law and Design.

title: Relational Context Legitimacy: A Trust-Based Framework for Ethical Personalization

detail.abstract: Personalization research has long framed consumer discomfort with data-driven marketing as a trade-off between relevance and privacy, producing compliance-driven solutions that treat trust as a legal threshold rather than a relational condition. This paper argues that the mechanism underlying consumer discomfort is not a calculus failure but a legitimacy failure: brands using data in ways the relationship has not earned the standing to support. Relational Context Legitimacy is introduced as a construct that names this mechanism, defined as the degree to which a brand's use of consumer data is warranted by the relational standing established through prior exchanges. Grounded in social exchange theory and the relational psychology of legitimacy, the construct separates legal permission from relational warrant and identifies the breach between them as the source of what consumers experience as surveillance in personalization. The construct is differentiated from contextual integrity and positioned within the Customer Trust Equation as a diagnostic filter determining whether personalization adds Connection and Value or introduces Friction into the consumer-brand relationship. Spotify Wrapped is examined as an illustration of Relational Context Legitimacy honored in practice. Implications are developed for practitioners, through the earned context decision heuristic, and for researchers, including directions for empirical validation using consumer-brand trust data. A brand earns the standing to use consumer data through the relationship itself, not through policy compliance alone, and personalization built on that standing compounds trust instead of wearing it down.

title: Identifying a Robust Risk-Return Relation
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Identifying a Robust Risk-Return Relation
detail.abstract: Is there a risk-return tradeoff in aggregate stock markets? This paper argues that the difficulty of answering this question reflects not only low power, but also finite-sample fragility: when return variance is the regressor, conventional OLS inference can depend disproportionately on a small number of especially noisy observations. These statistical challenges motivate the use of more efficient and robust estimators, direct forward-looking measurement of conditional risk from option-prices, and an expanded testable dataset covering global markets. Combining these methods and data, I document a robust, significant and economically meaningful relation between risk-neutral variance and subsequent realized market returns. Local market risk not only predicts returns within countries over time, but also explains differences in market returns across countries. A forecast of risk-neutral variance that is based on realized variance extends U.S. evidence back to 1885. Overall, the results reveal a stronger, more systematic relationship between conditional risk and stock market returns over time and across countries than previously recognized.

title: Capturing Heterogeneity: Machine Learning Approaches to Implied Volatility Forecasting
affiliations: and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Capturing Heterogeneity: Machine Learning Approaches to Implied Volatility Forecasting
detail.abstract: Despite documented heterogeneity in volatility dynamics across the option surface, standard implied volatility forecasting models apply homogeneous parameters throughout. We introduce a machine-learning framework that uses regression trees to partition the surface along both moneyness and maturity dimensions, identifying data-driven regions where distinct forecasting models perform best. Extending the Surface Heterogeneous Autoregressive (SHAR) framework of Dufays, Jacobs, and Rombouts (2025), we develop tree-based SHAR specifications that preserve interpretable structure while allowing model parameters to vary across the surface. Empirical analysis using S&P 500 options demonstrates that the boosted tree-based specification achieves the lowest out-of-sample forecast errors across all horizons, reducing one-month-ahead RMSE by 13% versus the benchmark SHAR model. The improvements are statistically significant and particularly pronounced during stress periods. The estimated tree presents economically interpretable segmentation: short-dated options exhibit higher daily persistence but lower monthly persistence than long-dated options, while deep out-of-the-money calls or puts display distinct dynamics from near-the-money contracts.
