title: Delayed Price Adjustment Following Volatility Shocks in Equity Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Delayed Price Adjustment Following Volatility Shocks in Equity Markets
detail.abstract: We examine whether unexpected changes in implied volatility predict future S&P 500 returns using daily data spanning 1990-2026. Constructing standardized volatility shocks as normalized daily changes in the VIX index, we find no statistically significant return predictability at short horizons of one to three days. Predictability emerges robustly at five-and ten-day horizons, surviving Newey-West standard error correction and controls for lagged returns. Regime analysis reveals a striking sign reversal: volatility shocks positively predict next-day returns in high-volatility environments (β = 0.0005, p = 0.024) but negatively predict returns in low-volatility environments (β =-0.0002, p = 0.048). These findings are consistent with a delayed price discovery mechanism operating primarily during periods of market stress, where forced deleveraging temporarily depresses prices below fundamental value before gradual mean reversion follows.

title: Influence of the Farm Harvest Prices on Acreage and Income from Sugarcane Crop in Haryana State of India
affiliations: Near Goshala,Old Govt. Hospital, Tau Devi Lal Government College For Women, Chaudhary Devi Lal University and Chaudhary Devi Lal University

detail.title: Influence of the Farm Harvest Prices on Acreage and Income from Sugarcane Crop in Haryana State of India
detail.abstract:
Aim: The present study was carried out to examine the impact of farm harvest prices on the income
of the farmers from sugarcane crop in Haryana, India. It also addresses the critical issue of acreage
response to prices in the agricultural sector.
Materials and Methods: It pertains to the whole of the state of Haryana, and the data for area, prices,
yield, production, and income were collected, systematized and analyzed for the period 1982/83 to
2021/22 by dividing the whole study period into four periods. Farmers take decisions about crop
and quantity based on the crop prices that affect the area allocation for different crops. To evaluate
the acreage response concerning the price impact on relative profitability, the compiled data were
analyzed by performing the Nerlovian distributed lag method.
Results: The findings emphasize that price remained the most instrumental factor in comparison to
yield in increasing farm income from sugarcane crops. The examination of the relationship between
the price of sugarcane and other selected variables highlights that income has a higher degree of cor-
relation with the price of sugarcane.
Conclusions: In the majority of cases the relative crop of sugarcane, i.e., paddy was found more
profitable.

title: Relationship Between Environmental Changes and Waste Management Policies on the Formation of the Quality of Life in Poland. A Regional Approach
affiliations: The Jan Kochanowski University in Kielce and Cracow University of Economics

detail.title: Relationship Between Environmental Changes and Waste Management Policies on the Formation of the Quality of Life in Poland. A Regional Approach
detail.abstract:
Aim:
The aim of the study is to assess the impact of environmental change and waste management policies on the quality of life of county population in Poland, taking into account their spatial differentiation.

Material and methods:
The study applies statistical data analysis, a comparative approach to identify regional variation and determinants of change and synthetic measure (TOPSIS method). Statistical data was collected at the county level. The choice was related to the data availability in Statistics Poland for 2010–2020.

Results:
The results of the analysis show a stable level of quality of life with an upward trend, which indicates the effectiveness of social policy, but also the need for improvement in regions with lower welfare. Waste management remains stable, but further action is needed on recycling and infrastructure, and to reduce regional disparities. The state of the environment is deteriorating in areas with high urbanization and industrial development, highlighting the need for coordinated environmental policies.

Conclusions:
Environmental changes, such as climate change and pollution, affect the quality of life, especially in the context of regional inequalities. Waste management policies and green transformation are key to minimizing these impacts, promoting recycling and sustainability. While the quality of life and waste management remain stable, further efforts are needed to reduce inequality and improve the environment through investment in infrastructure and environmental education.

title: Keep the Black Box Black: A Benchmark-relative Method for Measuring Growth Efficiency
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Keep the Black Box Black: A Benchmark-relative Method for Measuring Growth Efficiency
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a benchmark-relative method for measuring growth efficiency. The starting point is the standard growth accounting identity: growth = factor input × efficiency. Factor input is further decomposed into hard elements (capital, labor, technology, infrastructure) and soft elements (institutions, culture, human capital, social trust)-a distinction supported by a body of Nobel Prize-winning work. The difficulty lies in measurement: neither the factor composition weight (w) nor efficiency (E) is directly observable. This paper does not attempt to estimate their absolute values. Instead, it fixes one and observes the other-fix E to infer w, then fix w to infer E. All values are interpreted relative to a baseline, not as absolute quantities. In growth accounting, the residual-what cannot be explained by measured inputs-is often called a "black box." It is not a thing that can be opened; it is the limit of what can be observed. This paper does not try to open it. It keeps the black box closed and measures only the deviation of growth efficiency from a stable benchmark. Applied to five countries (2014-2023), the framework identifies patterns that correspond to observable real-world events: Irelands GDP distortions in 2018 and 2021, and Brazils higher hard-element efficiency relative to the US in 2022. The framework does not claim to measure efficiency more accurately. It claims to offer a different perspective-one that keeps the black box closed and asks a simpler question: compared with where we were, are we getting better or worse? This approach, while demonstrated in economics, provides a general strategy for measurement in domains where the observable and the unobservable are intertwined.

title: The Epistemological Crisis of Fordist Education: Studio Pedagogy, Production-Based Learning, and the Emancipatory Reconstruction of Professional Formation

detail.title: The Epistemological Crisis of Fordist Education: Studio Pedagogy, Production-Based Learning, and the Emancipatory Reconstruction of Professional Formation
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the lecture-examination model dominating contemporary higher education is not merely pedagogically inefficient but epistemologically misaligned with the demands of knowledgework economies. Drawing on critical pedagogy (Apple, 2004; Freire, 1970; Giroux, 1988; Hooks, 1994), Frankfurt School theory (Adorno & Horkheimer, 1944; Habermas, 1984, 1987), situated cognition research (Lave & Wenger, 1991), social realist philosophy of education (Archer, 2000, 2003), and the capabilities approach (Nussbaum, 2011; Sen, 1999), we contend that the Fordist model of passive content consumption followed by episodic assessment was designed for an industrial economy that no longer exists. We develop the concept of the Epistemological Crisis of Fordist Education (ECFE) — the structural condition in which the means of institutionalised knowledge formation are systematically misaligned with the epistemic demands of the social and economic contexts that education is called upon to serve — distinguishing it from adjacent concepts including Bourdieu’s misrecognition, Habermas’s legitimation crisis, and Apple’s curriculum ideology. We deploy Archer’s morphogenetic framework to analyse how educational structures generate emergent properties that condition human formation across generational time. We examine three historical precedents — Athenian paideia, Renaissance studio apprenticeship, and the Oxbridge tutorial — to demonstrate that production-based learning is not a contemporary innovation but a recovery of educational forms suppressed by the Fordist mass university. We theorise the studio pedagogy model as an emancipatory reconstruction of professional formation, grounded in the Carnegie Foundation’s Preparation for the Professions research programme (Benner et al., 2010; Cooke et al., 2010; Foster et al., 2006; Sheppard et al., 2008; Sullivan et al., 2007), the deliberate practice literature (Ericsson, 1993, 2016), and authentic assessment theory (Wiggins, 1990). Counterarguments concerning meritocracy, standardisation, scalability, and neoliberal co-optation are engaged at length. The paper concludes that ECFE is not a peripheral curriculum problem but a structural condition requiring architectural rather than cosmetic response.

title: Parallel Universe
affiliations: Independent and Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA)

detail.title: Parallel Universe
detail.abstract: This paper examines the economic and legal implications of parallel import restrictions in the United Kingdom. Parallel imports are genuine products imported without the consent of intellectual property rights holders, typically in response to price differences between markets. The authors argue that existing restrictions, inherited largely from European Union regulations, enable market segmentation and price discrimination, resulting in higher costs for consumers and public services. Drawing on evidence from the United Kingdom and other jurisdictions, the paper contends that abolishing most restrictions on parallel imports would increase competition, lower prices, expand consumer choice, and improve supply chain resilience. While acknowledging limited exceptions, particularly in relation to low-cost pharmaceuticals intended for developing countries, the authors advocate a return to a regime of international exhaustion of rights. They conclude that liberalizing parallel import rules would remove an unnecessary trade barrier and enhance economic welfare in post Brexit Britain.

title: Destroy or Resell? Product Returns, Disposition Choice, and the Economics of Destruction Bans

detail.title: Destroy or Resell? Product Returns, Disposition Choice, and the Economics of Destruction Bans

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is theoretical and computational. It involves no human participants, animal subjects, or identifiable personal data, and therefore ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: American consumers returned roughly $890 billion of merchandise in 2024, and undercover investigations have documented unsold and returned goods being routed to destruction at a reported rate of more than a hundred thousand items per week in a single warehouse. Regulators are responding in kind: France has required unsold non-food goods to be reused, donated, or recycled rather than destroyed since 2022, and the European Union's destruction ban for apparel takes effect in July 2026. Yet we are not aware of any formal equilibrium analysis of what such statutory bans do. This paper provides one. A two-period seller faces statutory no-questions-asked returns and chooses, unit by unit, whether to salvage (destroy) returned goods or refurbish and resell them alongside new units. Three results organize the economics. First, the privately optimal disposition rule is a quality-adjusted cost comparison, refurbish if and only if cδ > k + s, so destruction concentrates among high-markup, low-marginal-cost products. The familiar contrast between luxury houses that burn returns and electronics makers that run certified-refurbished programs falls out of a single threshold, unchanged across the valuation distributions we examine. Second, the welfare distortion decomposes across two margins. Whether to destroy is governed by the same threshold for the monopolist, a competitive industry, and a planner who ignores externalities, so within the model destruction is a cost verdict rather than an exercise of market power. Market power distorts how much is refurbished when returns are abundant (exactly half the efficient target under uniform valuations), and the environmental externality e creates a band of socially excessive destruction. Third, the policy consequences are sharper than current rule-making assumes. A destruction ban improves welfare only if e exceeds a closed-form threshold e* that increases in refurbishing cost; because banning destruction turns returns into liabilities, the ban raises the period-1 price and hurts the consumers whose returns it processes. A Pigouvian destruction tax weakly dominates the ban at every feasible point of a six-dimensional verification grid, coinciding with it where the taxed firm clears its returns voluntarily and avoiding the ban's far larger losses where forced clearance is wasteful. Yet under market power even the Pigouvian tax can lose to doing nothing, so the operative policy frontier is e*(k), and conditional on intervening, the tax is the regret-minimizing instrument. When return policies are endogenous, a calibrated extension shows a ban inducing the seller to devalue the consumer's return option, squeezing the balloon rather than shrinking it. A calibrated reading of the model rationalizes the EU's decision to target textiles first, and cautions against extending the ban to categories where refurbishing is costly.

title: Adapting Under Pressure: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Study of Psychological Distress and Resilience in First-Year Hellenic Air Force Cadets

detail.title: Adapting Under Pressure: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Study of Psychological Distress and Resilience in First-Year Hellenic Air Force Cadets
detail.abstract: Military academy training represents a uniquely demanding developmental context, combining the stressors of military socialization with academic pressure. This study examined trajectories of psychological distress and resilience in 92 first-year cadets (67.4% male) at the Hellenic Air Force Academy across three time points: entry in the academy (T0), post-basic training (T1, ~1 month), and end of the first semester (T2, ~5 months). Distress (DASS-21) and resilience (CD-RISC-25) were assessed longitudinally, alongside baseline personality (BFI-44) and Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB) at T2. Group-level analyses indicated significant reductions in distress and increases in resilience over time (all p ≤ .040), with basic training emerging as the primary period of change. Latent growth modeling revealed substantial individual variability, identifying heterogeneous adjustment trajectories. Cross-lagged panel models showed that higher distress predicted lower subsequent resilience (β =-.223 to-.286, p < .05), whereas resilience did not predict later distress. However, random intercept CLPM analyses indicated that these effects were attributable to stable between-person differences rather than within-person temporal dynamics. Personality analyses demonstrated that Neuroticism predicted higher subsequent distress (β = 0.479, p = .030), while Conscientiousness exerted a protective effect partially mediated by resilience (ab =-0.421, p = .017). Resilience at T2 was strongly associated with OCB (r = .564, p < .001), highlighting its functional relevance for organizational effectiveness. Overall, findings identify basic training as a sensitive window for psychological adaptation, underscore the importance of distinguishing within-and between-person processes, and support resilience as a key target for intervention in military education contexts.

title: The Corporate Playbook
affiliations: Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA)

detail.title: The Corporate Playbook
detail.abstract: The Corporate Playbook examines the growing tendency of corporations to engage in social, political, and environmental advocacy beyond their traditional commercial roles. The paper argues that stakeholder capitalism and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) initiatives have encouraged firms to pursue objectives that may conflict with shareholder interests and dilute corporate accountability. Through historical analysis and contemporary case studies, the authors contend that corporations increasingly adopt activist positions in response to pressure from investors, regulators, employees, and advocacy groups. The paper explores the economic and institutional implications of this shift, assessing its effects on competition, consumer welfare, and corporate governance. It concludes that businesses should prioritize value creation and remain cautious about assuming broader societal responsibilities that are more appropriately addressed through democratic institutions and markets.

title: Recommendation Capture: Adversarial Optimization, the Verification Vacuum, and the Hollowing of AI Product Recommendation

detail.title: Recommendation Capture: Adversarial Optimization, the Verification Vacuum, and the Hollowing of AI Product Recommendation
detail.abstract: Generative search interfaces are marketed on a single promise: the user no longer has to compare options, because the model has already done it. This paper argues that the same promise creates the incentive to corrupt the answer, and that a formalized optimization industry already does so at scale. Generative engine optimization, the practice of engineering content so that language models cite and recommend a product, derives much of its measured effectiveness from the manufacture of authority signals rather than from product merit. When every competitor in a category runs the same play, the model's reported best tracks the best optimizer, a quantity orthogonal to whether the product is good. I name this condition recommendation capture, by analogy to regulatory capture: an arbiter sold as neutral comes to serve whoever optimizes hardest, against the buyer it claims to serve. I argue that the resulting harm concentrates in a verification vacuum, the set of product categories where no independent ground truth exists, so that the model's recommendation is wholly a function of optimization, and that these categories tend to be the niche, the new, and the health adjacent, where vulnerable buyers are least able to check. Because models increasingly read the same open web that optimization floods, the corrupted output becomes the next input, and the interface erodes the trust it depends on. I sketch a tiered liability picture under existing false advertising and unfair practices law, identify which elements survive and which are untested, and argue that the deeper failure is one of market integrity and epistemics that current governance is structurally unable to detect.

title: Kristiansen's Theorem, Generalized Gamma Convolutions, and the Riemann Wald Couple
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Kristiansen's Theorem, Generalized Gamma Convolutions, and the Riemann Wald Couple
detail.abstract: Kristiansen's proof of Steutel's conjecture that a scale mixture of Γ(α) laws is infinitely divisible for every mixing measure if and only if α is between 0 and 2 endows the completed Riemann ξ-function with an unconditional infinite-divisibility oor, since its Pólya kernel is exactly Γ(2). We study the precise gap between infinite divisibility (ID) and membership in Thorin's class of generalized gamma convolutions (GGC), the class whose positivity is equivalent to the Riemann Hypothesis (RH). Writing the logarithmic derivative of a Laplace transform, ID is the complete monotonicity of ρ and GGC is the stronger Stieltjes property; equivalently, with k the canonical density, and GGC iff completely monotone. We exhibit an explicit two-atom Γ(2) mixture that is ID but not GGC, prove that no nite mixture is ever a GGC, and conclude that the GGC tier is intrinsically a continuum property. title: Nowcasting Italian Airfare Inflation: Identifying Index Weights from High-Frequency Digital Fares
affiliations: University of Tuscia, Bank of Italy, Luibao Limited and Università degli studi della Tuscia

detail.title: Nowcasting Italian Airfare Inflation: Identifying Index Weights from High-Frequency Digital Fares

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the project "Digital Innovation in Price Statistics: Open and Fast Insights from Online Scraped Data", under the PRIN 2022 call funded by the European Union – NextGenerationEU, Grant number J53D23004670006.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the nowcasting of monthly inflation for the Italian Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) sub-index Passenger transport by air using high-frequency ticket quotes collected from the Amadeus travel application programming interface (API). Our empirical contribution is to treat the absence of publicly available elementary weights as an identification problem: given a fixed set of representative routes and booking horizons, we compare unweighted aggregation with constrained weight-optimization schemes designed to approximate the official index. The index is constructed with a multilateral Time Product Dummy model, estimated by weighted least squares. In a pseudo real-time experiment over April 2024-December 2025, we find that the preferred weighting structure is horizondependent: a constrained scheme with both lower and upper bounds performs best at the one-month horizon, while an upper-bound-only constraint performs best at the two-month horizon, consistent with the view that light regularization can improve robustness by limiting weight concentration. Residual bias appears related to systematic coverage gaps, notably the absence of Ryanair fares in the chosen data source, underscoring the importance of representativeness when using API and web data for official-statistics nowcasting.

title: Reimagining Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms: A Path to Climate and Development Synergy
affiliations: Australian National University (ANU)

detail.title: Reimagining Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms: A Path to Climate and Development Synergy
detail.abstract: The European Union (EU)'s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) imposes import charges tied to carbon intensity and is set for full enforcement by 2026. Although it aims to reduce global emissions, its one-size-fits-all structure risks penalizing developing nations that often lack financial and technical resources for rapid decarbonization. This article presents "CBAM-Plus," a framework that reinvests CBAM revenues in clean energy infrastructure, facilitates technology transfer, and recognizes non-pricing mitigation strategies. By bridging capacity gaps and channeling funds toward local development, CBAM-Plus seeks to promote decarbonization without reinforcing global inequities. As additional countries consider carbon border policies, measures that align climate objectives with development priorities are vital to preventing a new global carbon divide.

title: The Hart-Scott-Rodino Act at Fifty: Acquisition Patterns and Industry Dynamics
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), Boston University - Questrom School of Business, USC Gould School of Law, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) - Lally School of Management and

detail.title: The Hart-Scott-Rodino Act at Fifty: Acquisition Patterns and Industry Dynamics
detail.abstract: The Hart-Scott-Rodino (HSR) Act requires firms to notify the U.S. antitrust agencies of acquisitions that exceed size thresholds. We study the economic consequences of the 2000 HSR Amendments, effective in 2001, which raised the minimum reporting threshold from $15 to $50 million, as adjusted, and removed the percentage-of-shares trigger, exempting many smaller transactions from review. Using SDC/Refinitiv transaction data, annual HSR reports, and Census Business Dynamics Statistics, we construct an industry-level measure of exposure to the reform and compare more-and less-exposed industries over the following two decades. We document three stylized facts: the HSR reform is associated with a shift in the composition of recorded acquisitions toward larger, same-industry, and repeated-acquirer deals; these responses differ sharply between goods-producing and service industries; and so do the accompanying changes in industry and labor-market dynamics.

title: The Prevalence Paradox in AI Radiology Triage: A General Decision-Analytic Framework

detail.title: The Prevalence Paradox in AI Radiology Triage: A General Decision-Analytic Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research received no external funding.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This is a theoretical decision-analytic framework using hypothetical and illustrative parameter values; no patient data, human subjects, or animal subjects were involved.

detail.abstract: Every hospital administrator evaluating an artificial intelligence radiology triage system asks the same question: for which diseases does the investment pay off? The intuitive answer is to deploy technology where disease is common, under the assumption that high prevalence maximizes true positives, improves workflow efficiency, and yields a stronger institutional return. We demonstrate that this reasoning, while straightforward, overlooks a fundamental prevalence-dependent cost reversal inherent to sequential filtering architectures. We develop a closed-form decision-analytic framework comparing humanonly interpretation and autonomous triage as explicit algebraic functions of disease prevalence, deriving the exact break-even threshold at which the two strategies match in expected cost per patient. Decomposing each cost function into fixed and variable components reveals the structural source of this economic inversion. Triage maintains a lower fixed cost floor by substituting a cheaper software fee for the human reading fee across the healthy majority, but introduces a steeper variable cost slope. This slope acceleration occurs because triage compounds false-negative probabilities across two classifiers in sequence, accumulating expected missed-diagnosis liabilities faster than human-only reads as disease prevalence rises. Below the break-even threshold, fixed cost savings dominate; above it, variable sequential error penalties dominate, rendering triage more expensive than human-only interpretation. We characterize the boundary behavior of this framework at economic extremes, derive the slope ratio between cost functions as a universal measure of the reversal severity, and provide a ceteris paribus sensitivity analysis for institutional customization. Ultimately, triage is most cost-effective for rare conditions and least cost-effective for common ones, a structural rule that requires no empirical calibration to establish.

title: Fund More, Fly Less: A Hybrid Meeting Cycle for More Effective and Equitable Climate Governance
affiliations: Australian National University (ANU)

detail.title: Fund More, Fly Less: A Hybrid Meeting Cycle for More Effective and Equitable Climate Governance
detail.abstract: The annual United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change's Conference of Parties (COP) has long served as a keystone of global climate diplomacy. However, concerns are growing that its current format may be increasingly resource-and carbon-intensive, and could limit the meaningful participation of low-income groups. This Perspective proposes a hybrid reform to the COP cycle: biennial in-person summits alternating with virtual thematic sessions in intervening years. This reform would redirect financial and institutional resources toward more inclusive participation and frontline climate action, particularly in the Global South. It offers a timely opportunity to realign global climate diplomacy with efficiency and impact.

title: The Transformation of Russian Coal Exports: Global Demand Trends and Market Positions in China and India
affiliations: Gaidar Institute for Economic Policy and Gaidar Institute for Economic Policy

detail.title: The Transformation of Russian Coal Exports: Global Demand Trends and Market Positions in China and India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Authors have no persoanl or financial relationship with other people or organizations
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research does not require ethics approval
declarations.funderStatement: Gaidar Institute funded this research project

detail.abstract: Analysis of forecasts by the International Energy Agency (IEA), the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), and BP indicates a consensus on the long-term trend of declining global coal consumption, with consumption peaking no later than the early 2030s. China is the main driver of this decline. At the same time, Russian coal exports are facing mixed trends in two key Asian markets. In China, Russia’s competitive position is weakening in the thermal coal segment but remains strong and is growing in the higher-margin coking coal segment, where Russia occupies an intermediate niche between cheap Mongolian and expensive Australian coal. In India, by contrast, Russian exports are showing steady growth thanks to a significant price advantage. However, further expansion is hampered by sanctions and logistical risks, as well as India’s import substitution policy, which aims to reduce coal purchases. Thus, to preserve Russia’s export potential, a consistent reorientation toward markets and segments with stable demand (coking coal in China and India) is necessary, while simultaneously diversifying logistics routes and removing tariff barriers.

title: The Artisan Paradox: Effort Signaling, Market Bifurcation, and Workforce Implications of Generative AI
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Artisan Paradox: Effort Signaling, Market Bifurcation, and Workforce Implications of Generative AI

declarations.funderStatement: The author declares no conflict of interest. No funding was received for this research. This paper was produced independently and does not represent the views of any institution, organization, or employer

detail.abstract:
The majority of current articles, academic papers and policy discussions focus exclusively on aggregate labour metrics, asking relatively predictable questions like ‘Will AI take my job?’ This narrow focus is a major blind spot. 

In my opinion, the real economic frontier in the age of automation is not just about whether a specific job survives, it is a psychological and structural rewrite of how human beings define worth. Market actors leverage high-quality presentation as a costly signal to communicate unobservable competence to uninformed parties  Researchers are ignoring how consumers completely restructure their valuation metrics when that signal is differentiated from actual human labour. This paper fills that gap by looking past employment statistics to analyse how consumer behaviour and pricing power shift when technical execution is transformed from a signal of quality into a free commodity.

title: Closed Circles: Is AI Infrastructure the Next Systemic Risk?
affiliations: William & Mary Law School

detail.title: Closed Circles: Is AI Infrastructure the Next Systemic Risk?
detail.abstract:
Global AI infrastructure investment is projected to exceed $5 trillion by 2030. In 2026 alone, U.S. tech groups’ AI-specific outlays are expected to total  2.1% of GDP — more than the relative cost of the railroads, interstate highway system, and Apollo space program. One of the largest capital cycles in history is being led by a small group of tightly held firms operating largely outside the regulatory perimeter. That makes one of the most important policy questions of the decade strikingly simple: what happens if things go south?

The inquiry has been missing from the literature. AI-focused legal scholarship has largely focused on the software story while financial-regulatory scholarship has not yet grappled with the potential that AI infrastructure may create systemic risk.

This Article fills that gap with two original empirical analyses. The first uses a novel methodology and data set to systematically map the AI infrastructure sector's most significant financial relationships. It surfaces structural features with financial-stability concerns, including circular transactions and unsustainable contractual commitments masked by uniformly low disclosure quality. The second analysis shows that the AI buildout is being financed not only by borrowing and investment, but also by accounting adjustments that soften near-term costs while boosting earnings by hundreds of billions.

Assessment of recent financial calamities – the late-1990s telecommunications overbuild and pre-2008 structured-finance wave – finds that the AI infrastructure build out simultaneously exhibits dangerous aspects of both. The Article suggests a calibrated regulatory response focused on enhancing disclosure, right sizing the regulatory perimeter and improving macroprudential supervision.

The central claim is not that a crash is inevitable, but that today's funding models and policy choices are generating the conditions under which one could occur – and that existing frameworks are poorly equipped to detect the risks or contain the resulting externalities.

title: Exchange Rate Risk and Exposure: Concepts, Determinants, Management Strategies, and Corporate Implications Hani

detail.title: Exchange Rate Risk and Exposure: Concepts, Determinants, Management Strategies, and Corporate Implications Hani
detail.abstract: In the era of globalization, international trade and cross-border investments have increased significantly, exposing businesses to various financial risks, particularly exchange rate risk. Exchange rate fluctuations can influence corporate cash flows, profitability, competitiveness, and overall firm value. This article examines the concept of exchange rate risk and exchange rate exposure, identifies the major factors contributing to exchange rate volatility, discusses strategies for managing foreign exchange risk, and analyzes the implications of exchange rate movements on corporate performance. The study employs a descriptive literature review approach by synthesizing theories and findings from international finance literature. The results indicate that exchange rate risk is an unavoidable aspect of international business activities, and effective risk management through financial and operational hedging strategies is essential for maintaining corporate stability and competitiveness in global markets.

title: Notes on the Categorial-logic of Capital

detail.title: Notes on the Categorial-logic of Capital
detail.abstract: The validity of the "method applied in Capital " as an external toolkit is one of the main issues that follows the publication of the first volume in 1867. The proposal presented here is based on the premise that this problem rests on a basic formal misunderstanding of the Marxian legacy. The hypothesis herein is as follows: the presentation found in Capital imposes that the method must conform to the object by the latter's necessity.

title: ToyBox-AI: e-commerce Toy Platform, Analysis & Research using UML  Diagrams

detail.title: ToyBox-AI: e-commerce Toy Platform, Analysis & Research using UML  Diagrams
detail.abstract: This research presents the analysis and design and research of ToyBox-AI, a web-based e-commerce platform for toy retail integrated with a rule-based conversational assistant. Traditional toy stores remain constrained by geographic limitations, manual ordering workflows, and the absence of automated customer support. ToyBox-AI addresses these gaps through a five module architecture covering profile management, toy browsing, order processing, payment handling, and a structured chatbot assistant. Using a UML-driven design methodology, this study models the complete system through ER, class, use case, activity, sequence, component, and hierarchy diagrams, providing a rigorous and replicable blueprint for implementation. The research demonstrates how systematic application of UML modeling produces a scalable, maintainable, and clearly documented architecture for intelligent toy retail management. Empirical usability evaluation of the implemented platform is identified as a concrete direction for future work, with a structured evaluation protocol proposed for subsequent studies.

title: Ecological Capitalism 3.0: A Market-Based Monetary Architecture for Systemic Biosphere Restoration

detail.title: Ecological Capitalism 3.0: A Market-Based Monetary Architecture for Systemic Biosphere Restoration
detail.abstract: All existing approaches to the ecological crisis share a structural limitation: they depend on continuous political will, international coordination, or voluntary behavioral change. This paper presents Ecological Capitalism 3.0 (EC 3.0), a monetary-ecological architecture that makes biosphere restoration economically more profitable than destruction-without requiring legislation, international agreements, carbon taxes, or altruistic actors.

title: Emerging Hybrid Monetary-Fiscal Framework: Supply-Side Sound Money Economics (SSSM) -Institutional Signals, Historical Parallels, and Illustrative Scenario Analysis (2026)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Emerging Hybrid Monetary-Fiscal Framework: Supply-Side Sound Money Economics (SSSM) -Institutional Signals, Historical Parallels, and Illustrative Scenario Analysis (2026)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not require ethics approval as it did not involve human participants, animal subjects, or the collection of sensitive personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Persistent post-2021 inflation, elevated U.S. debt-to-GDP ratios, and leadership changes at the Federal Reserve have exposed limits of the post-1971 discretionary monetary regime. This paper examines early signals from the second Trump administration and Chair Kevin Warsh's Federal Reserve (May 2026 onward) as evidence of an emerging pragmatic hybrid: Supply-Side Sound Money Economics (SSSM). The framework selectively combines supply-side incentives for output expansion, monetarist discipline on prices and balance sheets, and sound-money principles favoring market signals over discretion. We integrate primary statements, institutional actions, and macroeconomic data with historical parallels from the Volcker-Reagan era and illustrative forward scenario modeling through 2030. The analysis is conditional on early 2026 institutional signals, including internal reviews of communications, the balance sheet, data practices, productivity, and inflation frameworks. Descriptive comparative analysis shows that monetary restraint paired with supply-side measures has historically delivered lower inflation alongside subsequent growth recovery. Forward scenarios suggest that stronger implementation of balance-sheet normalization and supply-side alignment could facilitate inflation convergence near target while stabilizing debt dynamics, while limited progress would likely amplify existing risks. The paper highlights implementation risks and the "debt wall" constraint, and supports gradual, institutionally driven evolution toward the hybrid rather than abrupt regime change.

title: Regime-Dependent Synchronization of Mexican Regional Business Cycles with US and Chinese Industrial Shocks: A Markov-Switching Approach, 2005-2025
affiliations: Universidad Anáhuac México Norte and Universidad Anahuac Mexico

detail.title: Regime-Dependent Synchronization of Mexican Regional Business Cycles with US and Chinese Industrial Shocks: A Markov-Switching Approach, 2005-2025

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: This paper examines regime-dependent business cycle synchronization across all 32 Mexican states using quarterly ITAEE data from 2005Q1 to 2025Q3, combined with US Industrial Production (INDPRO), Chinese industrial output (PRINTO01CNQ663N), and state-level labor market data from MTPTREF. We estimate two-state Markov switching dynamic regression models independently for each state, fixed-effects panel regressions with cluster interactions, and a Filardo (1994) regime transition analysis. Five results emerge. First, all 32 states are synchronized with the US industrial cycle; full-sample correlations of ITAEE growth with US GDP growth range from 0.63 to 0.79, averaging 0.73 for maquiladora states and 0.71 for nearshoring statesmore than four times the corresponding China correlations. Second, Markov switching models converge for all 32 states and identify persistent asymmetric regimes with recession durations of 3 to 4 quarters and expansion durations exceeding 10 years. Third, the post-2022 tariff shock generated a statistically significant 2.3 percentage point acceleration across all state clusters, but without differential concentration in manufacturing statesconsistent with investment gestation lags. Fourth, manufacturing labor productivity is declining in both the traditional maquiladora cluster (-0.00222 per quarter, p=0.051) and the nearshoring cluster (-0.00117 per quarter, p=0.048), while manufacturing real wages rise uniformly at policy-determined rates; the maquiladora decline predates the 2019 minimum wage acceleration by fourteen years, placing the origin in the structural design of enclave manufacturing. Fifth, the regime transition analysis reveals that Chinese industrial expansion suppresses nearshoring state expansion probabilities with greater statistical precision (p=0.001) than maquiladora states (p=0.087), inverting the assumption that the new industrial cluster is less exposed to Chinese competition.

title: Residential Mobility Responses to Local Tax Cuts: Evidence from a Metropolitan City in Japan
affiliations: Musashi University and Nagoya City University

detail.title: Residential Mobility Responses to Local Tax Cuts: Evidence from a Metropolitan City in Japan
detail.abstract: This study examines how a permanent local tax cut affects metropolitan adjustment through residential mobility, asset markets, and local public finances, in a setting with enhanced local tax autonomy. We exploit a setting created by Japan's fiscal decentralization reform, in which a single municipality introduced a discretionary tax reduction within an otherwise uniform nationwide local tax system. Using the synthetic control method combined with origin-specific in-migration data, we analyze residential mobility and distinguish relocation across nearby administrative jurisdictions from broader interregional migration. The results show that the tax cut induces a relative increase in in-migration from within the same prefecture and neighboring prefectures, with persistent effects, but no statistically significant change in in-migration from other major metropolitan prefectures. These localized mobility responses are followed by gradual increases in residential land prices and property tax revenues, consistent with capitalization mechanisms emphasized in urban spatial equilibrium frameworks. Although these effects partially offset the fiscal impact of the tax reduction, they do not generate revenues beyond what would have occurred in the absence of the reform.

title: Risk Attribution in Rebalanced Characteristic Portfolios

detail.title: Risk Attribution in Rebalanced Characteristic Portfolios
detail.abstract: A rebalanced characteristic portfolio is a constructed object, but asset-pricing tests often attribute its exposure to the static label used to name it. Monthly rebalancing creates implementation roles: incumbents, entrants, exits, and boundary-crossing stocks through which the rule is actually held. This paper develops a role-based attribution correction and shows, in a pre-specified strict-OOS test block and a longer stress-rich evaluation block within one fixed pricing system, that the Baa-Aaa state-price component is located in boundary-crossing transition stocks rather than in the static liquidity label. The correction matters for risk attribution, benchmark construction, and portfolio monitoring because portfolio construction can change which stocks an asset-pricing test actually prices.

title: Bank Stocks and Multifactor Models
affiliations: Texas A&M University - Department of Finance,  Texas A&M University, Illinois Institute of Technology and University of Karachi - Institute of Business Administration (IBA), Karachi

detail.title: Bank Stocks and Multifactor Models
detail.abstract: Multifactor models have been developed over time to price nonfinancial stocks. This paper investigates their ability to price widely-perceived anomalous bank stocks. Based on standard cross-sectional regression tests, we find that, as factors are added to multifactor models, their ability to price bank stocks substantially improves. Even so, a recently proposed two-factor model normally outperforms other multifactor models with relatively high goodness-of-fit and statistical significance. Further graphs of average mispricing errors confirm these findings. We conclude that traditional multifactor models well explain the cross section of average bank stock returns.

title: Fraud Detection in Nigerian Banking: Temporal, Behavioral, and Geographic Patterns in One Million Transactions
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Fraud Detection in Nigerian Banking: Temporal, Behavioral, and Geographic Patterns in One Million Transactions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research was conducted independently with no financial relationships with any organization that could influence the findings.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses a publicly available synthetic dataset (Owolabi, 2025) hosted on Kaggle under CC BY-SA 4.0 licence. No human participants were involved and no personally identifiable information was accessed. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. This study does not involve clinical trials.

detail.abstract: Nigeria's digital banking sector processed over one trillion naira in transactions during 2025, yet fraud continues to erode consumer trust and impose measurable financial losses on customers and institutions alike. Despite widespread investment in rule-based detection systems, older adults and digitally inexperienced users remain disproportionately vulnerable. This paper presents the first large-scale empirical analysis of fraud patterns across ten Nigerian commercial banks using one million transactions drawn from a representative simulation of Nigerian Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) data. This paper documents three principal findings. First, fraudsters exhibit time-aware velocity manipulation: transaction speeds drop 7-15% during business hours to evade detection, then surge 45-58% between midnight and 3 AM when victims are asleep. Second, mobile banking is the sole channel where fraudulent velocity exceeds legitimate velocity (+4.2%), constituting evidence of automated or bot-driven attacks. Third, fraud rates vary by as much as 3.6-fold for the same bank across geographic locations, challenging the industry assumption of uniform national risk. On the modelling side, a Random Forest classifier achieves AUC-ROC of 0.82, improving on Logistic Regression (0.70) while detecting 64% of fraud cases. The paper discusses the fundamental precision-recall tension in low-prevalence fraud detection (0.3% base rate) and offers a prioritized set of policy recommendations for Nigerian banks.

title: Remittances and Inclusive Growth: Evidence from the MENA Region

detail.title: Remittances and Inclusive Growth: Evidence from the MENA Region
detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of workers' remittances in promoting inclusive growth in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. Using panel-data techniques for Egypt, Morocco, and Tunisia over the period 1985-2014, the study investigates the relationships among GDP per capita, remittances, foreign direct investment (FDI), gross domestic savings, gross fixed capital formation, and labour-market participation. The empirical strategy accounts for cross-sectional dependence, panel unit roots, cointegration, and causality. The findings indicate a positive long-run relationship between remittances and growth in the selected MENA economies. The results suggest that the growth effects of remittances are likely to be stronger when financial markets are developed, macroeconomic policy is stable, and recipient economies create incentives for formal, productive, and sustainable remittance transfers.

title: Crate or Crib: (Some) Economics of Pet Ownership
affiliations: Claremont McKenna College, Claremont McKenna College - Robert Day School of Economics and Finance, Colby College - Department of Economics and University of Richmond - E. Claiborne Robins School of Business - Economics

detail.title: Crate or Crib: (Some) Economics of Pet Ownership
detail.abstract: From water bowls for dogs on restaurant patios to the booming pet "daycare" industry, pets play a historically unprecedented role in the American family of the 21st century. We channel Gary Becker in studying the economics of pet ownership and spending. We document how pet ownership and expenditure vary by household composition. Beyond specific anecdotes, we find examples of expenditure patterns consistent with pet owners treating their pets as one would treat a child. Our theoretical framework illustrates that pet ownership serves as a medium through which changes in other economic variables, such as the time cost of children and returns to experience, affect the timing of fertility and, ultimately, fertility rates themselves. Taken together, we argue that studying pet ownership is interesting not only in its own right but also for a more complete understanding of the economics of fertility.
